title: Asian  Currencies  Mixed Amid Risk-off Sentiment -- Market Talk
text:
2113 ET - Asian currencies are mixed against USD in the morning Asian session amid risk-off sentiment spurred by losses in regional equity markets. However, with major central bank risks out of the way, there could be little informational value in price action in coming days, TD Securities says. USD could consolidate against other currencies into year-end as FX markets work off some residual positioning and value excesses, the brokerage adds. USD/KRW edges 0.1% lower to 1,185.44 while USD/SGD is little changed at 1.3643 and AUD/USD is steady at 0.7181. (ronnie.harui@wsj.com)

1916 ET - Japanese stocks are lower, dragged by declines in electronics and pharmaceutical stocks, as the yen strengthens amid economic uncertainty over the Omicron variant. Lasertec sheds 2.1% and drug maker Eisai is 1.8% lower. Investors are focusing on the Bank of Japan 's policy decision later in the day, as other major central banks take steps toward tightening to curb inflation. USD/JPY is at 113.68, down from 114.15 as of Thursday's Tokyo stock market close. The Nikkei Stock Average falls 0.6% to 28888.20. (kosaku.narioka@wsj.com; @kosakunarioka)

1854 ET - The RBA has put three options to the money markets for the wind up of its QE program. In a speech by RBA Gov. Philip Lowe on Thursday, he indicated the central bank was keen to end things by May if possible, but he also left open the potential to exit QE entirely in February. ANZ says a February exit is coming given the strength of the job market and the economy more broadly. With November labor-market data coming in much stronger than the RBA expected, and a revision in other forecasts likely, an end to QE altogether in February is the most likely option in our view, ANZ says. (james.glynn@wsj.com; @JamesGlynnWSJ)

1725 ET - For Australian residential property developers, risks around further macroprudential intervention by regulators appear to be subsiding, Morgan Stanley says. Australia's Council of Financial Regulators has announced that it won't introduce more measures at this stage, beyond the existing 50-basis-points rise in serviceability buffers. "Our channel checks suggest that this measure has not had a material impact on sales rates, with inquiry levels continuing to increase in December," says Morgan Stanley , which remains overweight on both Stockland and Mirvac . (david.winning@wsj.com; @dwinningWSJ)

1648 ET - IGO 's A$1.1B acquisition of Western Areas can enable it to keep mining nickel for more than 10 years, Jefferies says. IGO is offering to buy Western Areas for A$3.36/share in cash, representing a 36% premium to the stock on Aug. 18, the day before its takeover interest became known. Jefferies estimates the deal will lift IGO 's annual nickel output to 39,000 tons in FY 2023. It also sees the deal boosting IGO 's Ebitda and EPS, but weighing on net present value. "With nickel being a key winner in the electric-vehicle battery demand thematic, a key question will be if this is the first and final offer or if more suitors will emerge," says Jefferies, which rates IGO at buy. (david.winning@wsj.com; @dwinningWSJ)

1647 ET - The IPC stock index closes up 0.4% at 51384 and the peso strengthens to 20.83 against the US dollar from 21.01 yesterday after the Bank of Mexico raised its policy interest rate by 50bp to 5.5% instead of the widely expected 25bp. Aeromexico sinks 52% as the airline said a third party will make a public offer at one Mexican cent on the peso to allow existing shareholders the chance to withdraw before a debt capitalization and capital increase as part of its Chapter 11 restructuring, which will substantially dilute existing holders. (anthony.harrup@wsj.com)

1617 ET - The Bank of Mexico 's 50bp interest-rate hike to 5.5% after four consecutive 25bp increases may be a one-time move, says Goldman Sachs' Latin America economist Alberto Ramos, adding that the next decision could be a 25bp increase or even a hold. He expects the central bank to raise the rate to 6.5% next year, but says it could wait until the Fed starts raising rates--probably in March--before resuming tightening, "particularly if there are no new negative inflation surprises and the balance of risks does not deteriorate further." (anthony.harrup@wsj.com)

1546 ET - US and Canadian companies registered less debt and equity to sell in the markets in November, CUSIP Global Services says Thursday. Requests for corporate CUSIP codes, which are akin to serial numbers for securities, fell 5.6% in November compared with the previous month, says CUSIP, which registers the codes. On a year-over-year basis, corporate CUSIP requests from North American companies rose 1.3%. (Nina.Trentmann@wsj.com; @Nina_Trentmann)

1431 ET - Seasonal holiday hiring jumped this year, staffing firm PeopleReady says. The number of part-time and flexible hour jobs are 47% higher than pre-pandemic levels. More than 2M part-time and flexible hour jobs have been posted between September and October of this year, compared to 1.2M for the same period in 2019. Jobs packing, shipping and delivering items along with hospitality-related positions are the most in demand. The continued growth of jobs in sectors like hospitality and warehousing are key indicators that this year's holiday season will continue to provide strong job opportunities for those seeking work, PeopleReady says. The most in-demand jobs this holiday season include restaurant servers, warehouse associates, package handlers and cleaners and housekeepers. (chris.wack@wsj.com)

1430 ET - Intelsat SA announces that it reached a settlement with a group of convertible noteholders who had previously refused to support the company's chapter 11 plan of reorganization. The dissenting creditors, which include Cyrus Capital Partners and Anchorage Capital Group, agreed to withdraw their objections and they will receive an additional $25M in cash recoveries as part of the settlement, on top of the $39M slated for distribution. Previously, the parent-company bondholders had alleged that Intelsat's directors chose a chapter 11 plan that unfairly rewarded a competing creditor group. Judge Keith L. Phillips of the Eastern District of Virginia said on Thursday he would approve the company's proposed reorganization plan following the withdrawal of the creditors' objections, paving the way to a non-contested exit from bankruptcy for the satellite company. (alexander.saeedy@wsj.com; @ajsaeedy)

1348 ET - Canada PM Justin Trudeau 's office releases letters he wrote to members of his cabinet outlining what their priorities will be. For Finance Minister Chrystia Freeland , Trudeau says one of her top jobs will be to raise the corporate tax rate paid by banks and insurance companies that earn more than C$1B in annual net profit. Trudeau promised a higher tax rate, 18% to 15%, for banks during his re-election campaign. Royal Bank of Canada CEO Dave McKay warned this month the Liberal government's pursuit of a higher bank surtax could hurt the country's effort to attract domestic and foreign capital, especially as Canada will require trillions to meet Trudeau's goal of net-zero emissions by 2050. (paul.vieira@wsj.com; @paulvieira)

1339 ET - The US dollar weakens 0.3% vs the euro and yen. The WSJ Dollar Index falls 0.3%. Dollar support is fading as a high beta rally extends, Bank of America says. "With the December FOMC meeting concluded, we flag with interest that our signals have broadly shifted away from USD and toward the higher beta segment of the FX spectrum," the firm says. "USD signals vs. EUR, CHF & JPY are roughly neutral." In the medium term, BofA says in a G10 FX strategy note it's bearish the dollar against all currencies but the Swiss franc. (jonathan.vuocolo@wsj.com; @jonvuocolo)

(END) Dow Jones Newswires

December 16, 2021 21:14 ET (02:14 GMT)

title: *S&PGR Affirms 'AA+/A-1+' Ratings On Queensland; Stable
text:
22 Sep 2021 02:11 ET  Press Release: S&PGR Affirms 'AA+/A-1+' Ratings On Queensland; Stable


 
 
The following is a press release from S&P Global Ratings: 
 
OVERVIEW 
     -- Queensland is recovering from COVID-19's shock to the economy. 
Significant fiscal stimulatory initiatives and a large infrastructure pipeline 
are improving economic growth but weighing on budgetary performance in the 
short term. 
     -- We expect operating margins and after-capital account deficits to 
strengthen from fiscal 2023 onward; however, debt levels will remain elevated 
due to the state's large capital program. 
     -- We are affirming our 'AA+' long-term rating on Queensland. The outlook 
is stable. 
     -- Our ratings on Queensland remain supported by its exceptional 
liquidity position as well as its wealthy economy and effective management. 
 
RATING ACTION 
MELBOURNE (S&P Global Ratings) Sept. 22, 2021--S&P Global Ratings affirmed its 
'AA+' long-term foreign currency and local currency ratings and 'A-1+' 
short-term issuer credit rating on the Australian state of Queensland. The 
outlook is stable. 
 
OUTLOOK 
The stable outlook reflects our expectation that Queensland will experience a 
significant and temporary COVID-19-induced hit to budgetary performance. This 
will improve as local and national economies recover and the government 
effectively manages its budget. Debt levels will rise in the meantime and 
remain consistent with the state's 'AA+' rated peers. 
 
Downside scenario 
We could lower our long-term ratings on Queensland if we believe its fiscal 
recovery from the COVID-19 recession will be delayed beyond our current 
expectations. This could be evidenced by operating margins and after-capital 
account deficits underperform our forecasts. 
 
Upside scenario 
Upward pressure could occur if budgetary performance improved markedly and 
total tax-supported debt declined substantially. This could occur if the 
government achieves strong operating surpluses that reduce its after-capital 
account deficits and borrowing needs. This could also improve our view of its 
financial management. 
 
RATIONALE 
We have updated and extended our forecasts for Queensland through to fiscal 
year 2024 following the publication of the state's 2021-2022 budget. We expect 
Queensland's operating position to revert to surplus in the outer years of our 
base case, supported by stronger revenues from an improving economic outlook. 
We expect after-capital deficits to persist as the state focuses on large 
spending initiatives, including a record infrastructure budget, to support 
health and economic outcomes. 
 
Debt levels should plateau as Queensland's budgetary performance begins 
moderating in fiscal years 2023 and 2024. We believe the state will maintain 
its exceptional liquidity position. 
 
Our ratings on Queensland are supported by the general strength and wealth of 
its economy. Queensland has to date successfully contained the spread of the 
virus, allowing its economy to open faster than its peers, notwithstanding a 
few recent COVID-19 cases. The state also benefits from an extremely strong 
institutional framework, and strong financial management. 
 
Economy recovering after short lockdowns; experienced financial management 
continues to support ratings 
Queensland's economy has started to recover from the shock of COVID-19-related 
lockdowns. The economy is outperforming the national average because the state 
has contained the spread of the virus to date. The road to recovery will be 
bumpy. The government expects Queensland's gross state product to have 
rebounded to 3.25% in fiscal 2021 and to grow at about 2.75% per annum until 
fiscal 2025. The state's labor market has driven this growth, with 
unemployment rates the lowest they have been in a decade and the participation 
rate above pre-pandemic levels. The state's A$3.34 billion Queensland Job Fund 
continues to support the state's labor market. Employment levels improved 
significantly and the unemployment rate fell to 5.6% in the June quarter of 
2021 compared with 7.6% in the same quarter a year earlier. 
 
Most of Australia's states have been reasonably successful in suppressing the 
spread of coronavirus, notwithstanding recent outbreaks in New South Wales and 
Victoria, where the Delta variant is communally spreading. Uncertainty around 
lockdowns, the slow pace of the vaccine rollout, and interstate border 
openings are weighing on consumer and business sentiment. Australia's 
international borders remain closed, hurting Queensland's services export 
sector. 
 
Queensland has a relatively diverse economy but is one of the world's largest 
coal and liquid natural gas exporters, which means changes in commodity prices 
can affect economic growth figures and revenue growth. While growth was 
robust, the pandemic hurt the market as global activity waned. Recent trade 
tensions with China have also had an effect. Coal exports fell about 9%-10% in 
fiscal 2021. The outlook is uncertain due to the current global scenario and 
growing trade tensions with China. However, agricultural and metal exports 
have remained resilient through the pandemic. 
 
Fiscal and monetary policy in Australia is now extremely accommodative. The 
federal government is delivering large stimulus and wage-subsidy programs, 
while the Reserve Bank of Australia  has kept its policy rate at its 
lowest-ever level of 0.10% and introduced an asset purchase program and term 
funding facility for the banking system. Recent interventions by Australia's 
central bank  will bolster liquidity. In November 2020, the reserve bank 
launched its first-ever program of quantitative easing. In July 2021, it 
announced the third round of its program, continuing to purchase government 
bonds at a weekly pace of A$4 billion, rather than the current A$5 billion. 
 
Supporting the state's strong financial management is the institutional 
framework within which all Australian states and territories operate. We 
consider this framework to be one of the strongest and most predictable for 
subnational governments globally. It promotes a robust management culture and 
high levels of disclosure and transparency. Queensland has a prudent approach 
of long-term planning and transparency, and exceptional debt and liquidity 
management through Queensland Treasury Corp . The government's Debt Action Plan 
successfully reduced the state's debt levels prior to the pandemic, by using 
long service leave assets and surplus assets in its defined benefit 
superannuation fund to reduce its borrowing needs. 
 
Fiscal metrics will improve as large infrastructure program driving debt 
higher; liquidity coverage remains exceptional. 
Queensland's budgetary performance will be weak over the next two years before 
improving. We project operating balances to be in deficit of about 2%-3% 
before reverting to surplus in fiscal 2023. Queensland's average operating 
balance is about 0.06% of operating revenues between 2020 and 2024. These 
metrics are better than our forecasts in December 2020 because the economy is 
recovering quicker than we previously forecast. Increased income from 
property-related taxes, payroll taxes, and goods and services taxation have 
improved the revenue outlook. We believe GST revenues will continue to grow 
over time as the national GST pool increases, notwithstanding headwinds in the 
current quarter due to lockdowns in other states. Meanwhile, the hardest hit 
revenue source of royalties and land rent revenue will rebound in fiscal 2022 
following a significant downfall 2021 led by lower coal and oil prices and a 
moderation in coal export volumes. 
 
Responding to the pandemic, the state government introduced its Savings and 
Debt Plan with the aim of achieving efficiencies of about A$3 billion over the 
next four years. It initiated a range of savings measures last year and has 
achieved A$750 million in savings over the last financial year. The state 
continues to focus on enhancing investment and facilitating private sector 
business growth to boost employment through its Queensland Jobs Fund. 
 
The state's large capital plan will keep its after-capital account in deficit. 
We forecast the deficit will average around 10% of total revenues for the 
foreseeable future, peaking at 13% of total revenues in 2021. The state's 
record infrastructure program is focused on various transportation related 
projects and social housing supply along with developing various health and 
education infrastructure. With record levels of infrastructure construction 
occurring across Australia, we believe there is some risk of cost overruns, 
skilled labor shortages, and project delays. Capacity constraints mean the 
state may struggle to deliver on its budgeted capital spending. Therefore, our 
forecasts assume only 90% will be delivered each year. 
 
We forecast total tax-supported debt to reach about 155% of operating revenues 
by the end of fiscal 2024, up from 124% in fiscal 2020. The state's rising 
debt burden is mainly a result of record levels of capital expenditure. That 
said, the state's debt levels compare well with its similarly rated domestic 
and international peers, which have been struck harder by the pandemic. 
Queensland's Debt Action Plan helped reduce the state's debt levels before the 
pandemic. 
 
On June 30, 2021, Queensland established the Queensland Future (Debt 
Retirement) Fund (DRF), for the purpose of future debt repayments. It was 
initially seeded with about A$7.7 billion of assets. Assets within the DRF 
will only be used to reduce debt and to pay associated administration 
expenses. The Queensland Future Fund Act 2020 provides the legislative 
framework for establishing and using the fund. This legislation was modelled 
on the legislative structure of the NSW Generation Fund Act 2018. Similar to 
the treatment applied to the NSW Generations Fund, we deduct a haircut amount 
of the DRF assets from our measure of tax-supported debt. We apply haircuts to 
the DRF's non-cash asset holdings, reflecting our view of credit and liquidity 
risks associated with these types of assets. We could reverse our analytical

approach if we observe any weakening in the government's commitment to the 
stringent rules that govern the fund. 
 
The state benefits from the current environment of low interest rates, with 
its interest expenses remaining below 5% of operating revenues. All Australian 
states have adopted new accounting standards to incorporate leases on to 
balance sheet as debt-like obligations. 
 
Queensland's liquidity coverage is comprehensive, reflecting its substantive 
liquid assets holdings, its strong access to external liquidity, and potential 
Commonwealth support if it was required. The debt-service coverage ratio is 
about 224% of upcoming debt maturities, interest costs and budget 
requirements. Queensland has about A$8 billion in debt maturing in the next 12 
months, including short-term notes. Queensland's liquid assets include its 
superannuation assets used to offset its upcoming superannuation liabilities 
because unlike other states that use trust accounts, Queensland directly 
manages these assets and can use them for liquidity purposes, if required. 
Further, we expect Queensland to continue to fully fund its superannuation 
liability. 
 
We consider the state has strong access to external liquidity. Similar to 
Germany and Canada, the Australian states utilize a well-developed capital 
market for their funding. The capital markets in Australia are deep and 
liquid, and we expect them to remain so. Queensland historically has had no 
difficulty in accessing Australian and international markets, and our 
expectation is that this will continue. 
 
Queensland's exposure to contingent liabilities is limited and do not weigh on 
our assessment of its credit metrics. The state is prone to natural disasters 
such as cyclones, floods, fires, and droughts, which present ongoing risks to 
its economy and budget. A significant proportion of these costs are met by 
Commonwealth Disaster Recovery Funding Arrangements (previously covered under 
the Natural Disaster Relief and Recovery Arrangements) and insurance.

title: *S&PGR Affirms Ratings On Australian State Of Victoria; Stable
text:
16 Aug 2021 00:15 ET  Press Release: S&PGR Affirms Ratings On Australian State Of Victoria; Stable


 
 
The following is a press release from S&P Global Ratings: 
 
OVERVIEW 
     -- Victoria is recovering from the economic shock caused by the COVID-19 
pandemic. Significant fiscal stimulatory initiatives and a large 
infrastructure pipeline are improving economic growth but weighing on 
budgetary performance over our forecasts. 
     -- The state will post large operating and after-capital-account deficits 
this fiscal year, elevating debt levels. 
     -- We are affirming our long-term rating on Victoria of 'AA'. The outlook 
is stable. 
 
RATING ACTION 
MELBOURNE (S&P Global Ratings) Aug. 16, 2021--S&P Global Ratings affirmed its 
'AA' long-term foreign currency and local currency ratings and 'A-1+' 
short-term issuer credit rating on the Australian state of Victoria. The 
outlook remains stable. 
 
OUTLOOK 
The stable outlook incorporates our expectation that Victoria's budgetary 
performance will remain in large after-capital account deficit and its debt 
levels will be elevated for years. 
 
Downside scenario 
We could lower our rating if Victoria's after-capital account deficits are 
wider than our forecasts. This could drive debt above our projections or 
structurally weaken the state's liquidity coverage. 
 
Upside scenario 
We could raise our rating if the economic recovery results in Victoria's 
fiscal metrics being considerably stronger than our forecasts. This could 
occur if the state achieved operating surpluses and reduced its after-capital 
account deficits materially arresting the rise in its debt. 
 
RATIONALE 
The COVID-19 outbreak and extended lockdown in Victoria in 2020 dealt the 
state a severe economic and fiscal shock compared with other states. We have 
updated and extended our forecasts for Victoria through fiscal year 2024 
following the publication of the state's 2021-2022 Budget. Victoria's 
budgetary performance will remain weak as it focuses on large spending 
initiatives, including a record infrastructure budget, to support health and 
economic outcomes. The state will continue to deliver operating deficits and 
wide after-capital account deficits over the coming years. Reflecting this 
weakening of fiscal outcomes, Victoria's debt levels will reach about 192% of 
operating revenues by the end of fiscal 2024. The state's debt levels will 
remain elevated for years. Although we see some prospect of fiscal repair, 
it's unlikely that it would occur within the next few years or substantially 
improve key financial metrics. 
 
Underpinning our 'AA' rating is our belief that economic growth is recovering, 
and the state's economy remains structurally wealthy and diverse on a global 
scale. Victoria's strong financial management should ensure that liquidity 
coverage is comprehensive during this period of disruption as the state 
progresses with its prefunding strategy. Australia's extremely supportive and 
predictable institutional framework continue to support our rating. 
 
Victoria's economy will recover when lockdowns lift 
Victoria's economy continues to possess strong fundamentals, despite economic 
contraction in the past fiscal year and the current lockdowns. Since the 
beginning of the pandemic, Victoria has had six lockdowns, including one in 
fiscal 2021 that lasted 112 days. The lockdowns have weighed on economic 
activity and growth. Postlockdown economic activity tends to rebound quickly, 
with the state anticipating real gross state product (GSP) growth of 6.5% in 
fiscal 2022 after an economic downturn in 2021 of -2%. The current lockdowns 
could drag on this expectation. State final demand rebounded 6.8% in the 
December quarter of 2020 after the extended lockdown, with easing of public 
health restrictions. The national economy is also starting to recuperate; we 
forecast it to grow 3.7% in 2021-2022. While the contraction in the last two 
quarters of fiscal 2020 was historically large, Australia is still 
outperforming most other advanced economies. 
 
Australia's states have been reasonably successful in suppressing the spread 
of coronavirus--notwithstanding recent minor outbreaks in Victoria and 
Queensland as well as a large outbreak in New South Wales, where the Delta 
variant is communally spreading. Uncertainty around lockdowns, the vaccine 
rollout, and interstate border openings are weighing on consumer and business 
sentiment. Australia's international borders remain closed, hurting Victoria's 
education and tourism industries. 
 
Despite the downturn, we expect Victoria will retain its economic strength, 
wealth, and diversity on a global scale. This remains a structural feature of 
the state. A large services sector and infrastructure pipeline and lifestyle 
appeal should support the state's long-term economic outlook. 
 
Victoria's unemployment rate was 4.4% as of June 2021. Commonwealth JobKeeper 
support ended in March 2021. The state has regained jobs lost at the height of 
the pandemic, with employment up 2.5% in 2021-2022. 
 
Victoria is the second-largest economy in Australia. It represents 3% of 
nation's land mass, accounting for close to a quarter of Australia's economic 
activity. Its populace is wealthy by international standards, with GSP per 
capita of around US$55,000. Its economy is services-driven and highly 
diversified. Victoria has about 6.6 million residents. We are anticipating 
population growth to dip in 2021 and 2022 because international borders remain 
largely shut, followed by a recovery beginning in 2022-2023. 
 
We view Victoria's financial management practices as being strong in a global 
context, though waning in recent years. We believe Victoria's control of 
operating expenses has moderately lagged other governments in the recent past, 
specifically in terms of wage outcomes and implementation of previous savings 
targets. We believe the state's commitment to costs control is important 
because it could alleviate some budgetary pressure that we are now seeing. 
Achieving the government's savings targets scheduled to commence in January 
2022 could also help. 
 
Although the pandemic has highlighted some differences in policy, Victoria, 
like all states, benefits from strong government administration and a system 
of checks and balances. The decision to lift public spending and investment 
should boost the economy and help businesses to recover. 
 
Victoria produces annual budgets that include detailed projections for three 
years beyond the budgeted fiscal year. It also produces midyear updates and 
audited final financial outcomes, generally within four months of period-end. 
Accounts are prepared on a cash and accrual basis, with public corporations 
consolidated. 
 
The state has revised its principles around net debt to a qualitative level to 
stabilize in the medium term, removing its quantitative limit on GSP. It is 
focusing on delivering operating surpluses before stabilizing debt levels. The 
state increased its net debt target to 12% from 6% of GSP to fund flagship 
projects and account for operating lease standard changes (AASB16). In our 
view, Treasury Corp. of Victoria  is well-managed and remains strong at 
managing the state's liquidity and debt. 
 
Supporting the state's management is the institutional framework within which 
all Australian states and territories operate. We consider this framework to 
be one of the strongest and most predictable for sub sovereign governments 
globally. It promotes a robust management culture and high levels of financial 
disclosure and transparency. 
 
Revenue write-downs, targeted fiscal stimulus, and a large infrastructure 
program will raise debt and continue suppressing budgetary performance 
The COVID-19 pandemic continues to weigh on Victoria's finances. We forecast 
the state's budgetary performance to significantly underperform its domestic 
and international peers. In our base-case forecast we expect operating 
deficits to peak at about 25% of operating revenues in fiscal 2021. While 
these will narrow, we expect them to remain in deficit until 2023 before 
achieving a small surplus in 2024. Victoria's average operating deficit is 
about 6.6% of operating revenues between 2020 and 2024. While these metrics 
are better than our forecasts in December 2020 because the economy has 
recovered quicker than we expected, they remain weak. Increased income from 
property-related taxes, payroll taxes, and goods and services taxation, along 
with revenue initiatives introduced in the current budget such as the Mental 
Health and Wellbeing Levy, have improved the revenue outlook, though the 
latter will increase expenses. 
 
The state is taking measures to achieve savings efficiencies after placing 
these plans on hold during the height of the pandemic. Departments have been 
tasked with delivering savings beginning in January 2022. Supporting fiscal 
recovery, we expect Victoria to receive A$2.3 billion in no-worse-off payments 
over the budget and forward estimates from the Commonwealth Government as part 
of horizontal fiscal equalization. 
 
The state's four-year A$74.3 billion capital plan will ensure the state's 
after-capital account remains in large and persistent deficit. We forecast the 
deficit will average more than 20% of total revenues for the foreseeable 
future, peaking at 45% of total revenues in 2021. The state's record 
infrastructure program is focused on needed transport projects, including 
roading, rail crossing removals, and public transport. Key projects in the 
pipeline include the Level Crossing Removal Program, North East Link, and 
Metro Tunnels. 
 
With record levels of infrastructure construction occurring across Australia, 
we believe there is some risk of cost overruns, skilled labor shortages, and 
project delays. Capacity constraints mean Victoria may struggle to deliver on 
its budgeted capital spending. Therefore, our forecasts assume only 85% will 
be delivered each year. 
 
We believe there is little meaningful upside to our base-case forecasts, given 
that Victoria's budgetary flexibility is similar to most of its domestic 

16 Aug 2021 00:15 ET 
Press Release: S&PGR Affirms Ratings On -2-


peers. The state hasn't announced any major balance sheet reforms such as 
asset recycling, which could narrow the deficit compared with our forecasts. 
 
Given the weak fiscal outlook, we expect debt to rise rapidly. We anticipate 
Victoria will increase its total tax-supported debt to A$164 billion, or 192% 
of operating revenues, in 2024 from A$78 billion, or 110% of operating 
revenues, in 2020. Debt levels are likely to continue rising beyond our 
forecast period. This rapid increase in debt means Victoria will have the 
highest total tax-supported debt as a proportion of operating revenues of all 
Australian states. We adjust Victoria's reported debt figures to nullify the 
A$7 billion central banking system. We classify the system as an internal 
transfer between government accounts. 
 
Despite its rising debt burden, Victoria's interest expenses remain low, at 
4.0% of operating revenues between 2021 and 2023. This is because of the low 
interest-rate environment. We believe Victoria's contingent liabilities are 
small compared with its peers and only a small portion, if any, is likely to 
crystallize. 
 
The state's liquidity remains sound, though its debt service coverage ratio 
has weakened due to its large operating deficit and infrastructure program in 
2022. The state's debt-service coverage ratio is about 12% of its upcoming 
debt maturities, interest costs, and budget needs. We anticipate liquidity 
metrics to improve to more than 40% of debt service in coming years as the 
state transitions through the large fiscal hit in 2021 and 2022. 
 
We consider the state to have strong access to external liquidity. The 
Australian states utilize a well-developed capital market for their funding. 
Victoria is a proven and established issuer in Australian and international 
markets. We also expect the Commonwealth to provide support, if needed, as it 
did during the 2008-2009 financial crisis. At the time, the Commonwealth 
provided a guarantee of Australian state government debt for a fee, though 
Victoria didn't take up this offer. 
 
Fiscal and monetary policy in Australia is now extremely accommodative. The 
federal government is delivering large stimulus and wage-subsidy programs, 
while the Reserve Bank of Australia  has kept its policy rate at its 
lowest-ever level of 0.10% and introduced an asset purchase program and term 
funding facility for the banking system. Recent interventions by Australia's 
central bank  will bolster liquidity. In November 2020, the reserve bank 
launched its first-ever program of quantitative easing. In July 2021, it 
announced the third round of its program, continuing to purchase government 
bonds at a weekly pace of A$4 billion, rather than the current A$5 billion.

title: *S&PGR Lowers New South Wales Long-Term Rating To 'AA+'; Stable
text:
7 Dec 2020 03:11 ET  Press Release: S&PGR Lowers New South Wales Long-Term Rating To 'AA+'; Stable


 
 
The following is a press release from S&P Global Ratings: 
 
OVERVIEW 
     -- The economic shock caused by the COVID-19 pandemic will see NSW lose 
billions of dollars in forecast revenue, while cushioning the economy through 
fiscal stimulus and a large infrastructure program. 
     -- The state will post historically large operating and 
after-capital-account deficits this fiscal year. As a result, debt will rise 
sharply, even if prospective asset sales eventuate. 
     -- We are consequently lowering our long-term issuer credit rating on NSW 
to 'AA+' from 'AAA'. At the same time, we are affirming our 'A-1+' short-term 
rating. The outlook is stable. 
     -- Our ratings on NSW are supported by its wealthy and diversified 
economy, which is recuperating from a recession in the first half of 2020; 
excellent financial management; and exceptional liquidity. 
     -- NSW was quick to control the spread of coronavirus, averting what 
could have been a deeper recession. It is well-placed to return to operating 
surplus and stabilize the balance sheet impact in the medium term. 
 
RATING ACTION 
MELBOURNE (S&P Global Ratings) Dec. 6, 2020--S&P Global Ratings today lowered 
its long-term issuer credit rating on New South Wales (NSW), an Australian 
state government, to 'AA+' from 'AAA'. At the same time, we affirmed our 
'A-1+' short-term rating. The outlook on the long-term rating is stable. 
 
OUTLOOK 
The stable outlook reflects our expectation that NSW's budgetary performance 
will improve during the next few years as the economy climbs out of a 
COVID-19-induced recession, and as it undertakes balance-sheet reforms to help 
fund a portion of its large infrastructure pipeline. New borrowings will see 
NSW's debt rise substantially, to levels consistent with 'AA+' rated peers. 
 
Downside scenario 
We see limited downside risk to our ratings on NSW in the next two years. 
Nevertheless, downward pressure could emerge if NSW underperforms our 
expectations, such that the operating deficits and large after-capital-account 
deficits become entrenched, resulting in a steeper rise in debt than presently 
forecast. This could occur, for instance, if NSW further expands its 
infrastructure program without concomitant revenue growth. Such developments 
might be evidence of weakening financial management. 
 
Upside scenario 
Upward pressure on the ratings could emerge if NSW's fiscal performance were 
to substantially exceed our expectations, with stronger after-capital-account 
balances. This could result in the state's debt burden falling well below our 
present forecast. 
 
RATIONALE 
The COVID-19 pandemic has dealt Australia's state governments a severe 
economic and fiscal shock. In the first half of 2020, the Australian and NSW 
economies plunged into recession for the first time in almost 30 years, though 
we believe that an upturn has now begun (see "Economic Research: Asia-Pacific 
Forecasts Stabilize, Risks Now Balanced," published Nov. 29, 2020). We have 
updated and extended our forecasts for NSW through fiscal year 2023 (i.e., the 
year ending June 30, 2023), following the release of the state government's 
annual budget in November 2020. 
 
The downgrade primarily reflects our expectation that NSW's debt burden will 
rise substantially during the next three years. We expect NSW to post a 
historically large after-capital-account deficit this fiscal year, though the 
deficit should narrow in future years. NSW has a higher degree of flexibility 
than its peers, with some potential upside to our deficit and debt projections 
from unbudgeted asset sales and expenditure reviews. 
 
Supporting NSW's rating at 'AA+' are its wealthy and diversified economy, 
excellent financial management, and exceptional liquidity. Its economy is on 
the mend after Australia's success in nearly eliminating local transmission of 
the coronavirus. 
 
Revenue writedowns, targeted fiscal stimulus, and a large infrastructure 
program will drive debt higher; liquidity coverage remains very strong 
The COVID-19 recession--and its lingering aftereffects--has had a severe 
effect on NSW's budgetary performance. NSW has written down its general 
government revenue forecasts over the four years to fiscal 2024 by A$14.8 
billion, relative to prepandemic expectations. At the same time, the state is 
rolling out tens of billions of dollars in economic support and stimulus 
initiatives and has further expanded its already-large forward infrastructure 
pipeline. We expect NSW to record a cash operating deficit of 12% in fiscal 
2021, before returning to balance shortly after as tax receipts rebound and 
emergency spending measures wind down. 
 
Multiple revenue lines have taken a hit. The largest loss of revenue will 
likely be from smaller goods-and-services tax (GST) grants from the 
Commonwealth government (i.e., the Australian sovereign) on the back of weaker 
domestic consumption. NSW forecasts that GST revenue over the next four years 
will be A$8.7 billion lower than anticipated prepandemic. Forecasts for 
receipts from payroll taxes, stamp duties, and mining royalties have also been 
written down. 
 
The fiscal recovery in future years will occur because NSW's stimulus measures 
are temporary and targeted, and an economic upturn has commenced. For 
instance, NSW will offer a two-year reduction in the payroll tax rate, 
forgoing A$2.1 billion in revenue. The response to the pandemic has also 
included more than A$3 billion in new spending to boost health system capacity 
and a A$3 billion Jobs and Infrastructure Acceleration Fund. 
 
In the medium term, we expect that NSW's strong commitment to fiscal 
discipline will limit growth in operating expenses. The November 2020 budget 
contains several new savings measures, the most important being A$4.3 billion 
saved from lower public-sector wages growth. This reflects a cap on wage 
increases of just 0.3% in fiscal 2021 for approximately 170,000 workers, 
rising to 1.5% for all public servants through fiscal 2024. 
 
The financial implications of a proposed reform of property taxes are 
uncertain, but likely to be manageable at the current rating. NSW is 
consulting on a proposal to phase out stamp duties and land taxes, replacing 
them with a new annual property tax. This proposal is not built into our 
base-case forecasts. On current modelling, there could be a loss of revenue of 
around A$11 billion over the first four years. However, in the longer run, the 
reform is designed to be revenue neutral. We think it could enhance 
productivity and make the state's taxation base less volatile. 
 
We expect NSW's after-capital-account deficit to widen to 36% of total 
revenues in fiscal 2021 before narrowing in subsequent years. NSW has 
announced a record multiyear infrastructure program, with capital expenditure 
(on a cash basis) forecast at around A$100 billion over the next four years. 
Around two-thirds of this figure is allocated to road, rail, and transport 
projects, with the remainder spread across health, education, and other areas. 
The NSW government estimates that capital investment will contribute one 
quarter of a percentage point to economic growth this year and support local 
employment outcomes. 
 
With record levels of infrastructure construction occurring across Australia's 
eastern states, we believe there is some risk of cost overruns, skilled labor 
shortages, and project delays. Capacity constraints mean NSW may struggle to 
deliver on its budgeted A$24 billion-A$28 billion of annual capital spending. 
As such, our forecasts assume an execution rate of about 90%. Our analysis is 
based on NSW's nonfinancial public sector, which consolidates the general 
government sector and government-owned corporations. 
 
While the state's infrastructure pipeline will be partially funded by 
financial assets previously accumulated in the NSW Infrastructure Future Fund, 
substantial new borrowing will be needed for future projects and to bridge the 
transitory operating deficits. We expect NSW's tax-supported debt to rise to 
about 149% of operating revenues by the end of fiscal 2023, up from 71% in 
fiscal 2019. These metrics are similar to its 'AA+' rated peers. The rise in 
public debt is a common theme across states except Western Australia (see 
"Shock And Ore: Surging Debt To Test Australian States," published Sept. 29, 
2020). 
 
The increase in NSW's reported debt includes a few billion dollars of leases 
as well as assets acquired using 'service concession' arrangements under a 
financial liability model. We note that under a recent accounting 
change--Australian Accounting Standards Board  (AASB) 16 Leases--there is no 
longer a distinction between operating leases and finance leases from fiscal 
2020 onward. Australia's public accounting standards in this regard appear to 
be more conservative than those of some foreign jurisdictions. 
 
In our measure of NSW's tax-supported debt, we subtract the balance of the NSW 
Generations (Debt Retirement) Fund (NGF), which stood at A$11.3 billion as of 
June 30, 2020. We do this because the sole purpose of the NGF, as articulated 
in the NSW Generations Funds Act 2018, is to set aside money to reduce future 
debt. This analytical treatment is unusual but consistent with our approach to 
the Province of Quebec in Canada, which has a similar sinking fund mechanism. 
 
The NGF will grow through investment earnings and future contributions. NSW's 
latest budget includes a commitment to direct dividends from state-owned 
corporations and mining royalties into the NGF. We don't yet know when the NSW 
government intends for the NGF to begin retiring debt. We could reverse our 
analytical approach if we observe any weakening in the state's commitment to 
the stringent rules that govern the fund. 
 
We assess NSW as having a better degree of budgetary flexibility than its 
peers because there is upside to our base-case forecasts from unbudgeted asset 
sales. In November 2020, the NSW government launched a sale process for its

remaining 49% stake in WestConnex, a tolled motorway. (The first 51% stake 
sold for about A$9.3 billion in 2018.) NSW has also announced a scoping study 
into the possible monetization of its lotteries duty revenue stream. 
Transaction proceeds from the former and possibly the latter will be deposited 
into the NGF, helping to reduce our measure of tax-supported debt. However, we 
still consider it likely that tax-supported debt will rise above 120% of 
operating revenues during the next few years, even with the benefit of 
prospective transactions. 
 
The NSW government has revamped its balance sheet during the past decade, and 
its strategy of "asset recycling" has helped to support new infrastructure 
investment while limiting growth in debt. The proceeds of past transactions, 
including full or partial divestments or concessions of Ausgrid , Endeavour 
Energy, and the state's property titling and registry services, have been 
recycled via the NSW Infrastructure Future Fund into new capital spending. 
 
NSW's liquidity remains robust. We estimate that its total free cash, 
including funding contracted since June 30, and after applying our standard 
haircuts to noncash financial assets, is sufficient to cover about 87% of debt 
service during the next 12 months. We expect NSW's debt-servicing needs to 
comprise about A$8.2 billion in short-term commercial paper borrowings, A$3.8 
billion and A$4.7 billion of term debt maturing in each of the next two fiscal 
years, and about A$3 billion-A$4 billion in annual interest expenses. We 
exclude from our measure of free cash the balance of the NGF as well as assets 
set aside to meet insurance and superannuation liabilities. 
 
We consider NSW to have strong access to external liquidity, reflecting its 
demonstrated history of issuing bonds in deep and liquid capital markets. 
Government bond yields in Australia have fallen to their lowest levels in 
history, in line with trends in many advanced economies. This will help to 
keep interest expenses manageable even as gross debt escalates. We also 
believe the Commonwealth government would provide support, if needed in a 
severe stress scenario, as it did in 2009-2010, when it offered a guarantee 
over state and territory government borrowing. 
 
Recent interventions by Australia's central bank  will bolster liquidity. In 
November 2020, the Reserve Bank of Australia  (RBA) launched its first-ever 
program of quantitative easing. It plans to purchase, among other assets, A$20 
billion of state and territory government bonds in the secondary market over 
the next six months. This complements an earlier series of bond purchases, 
which occurred over March 2020 to May 2020, that addressed market dysfunction 
but did not have an explicit quantity target. 
 
New South Wales Treasury Corp . (TCorp) manages the state's liquidity and 
external borrowings. Most of TCorp's outstanding debt issuance is in the form 
of Australian-dollar fixed-rate benchmark bonds, with a small volume of 
inflation-linked bonds, floating-rate notes, and foreign-currency notes. It 
uses swaps to fully hedge its foreign-currency exposures. TCorp has reduced 
refinancing risk by lengthening its maturity profile, and it actively engages 
in "switches" by buying back bonds nearing maturity and issuing at longer 
tenors. TCorp has also issued A$5.2 billion in green and sustainability bonds 
to date. 
 
NSW's contingent liabilities are small and do not weigh on our credit 
assessment. Quantifiable contingent liabilities for the general government 
sector stand at A$2.9 billion. Further, the borrowings of almost all 
government-owned corporations are already consolidated in our measure of 
tax-supported debt. However, NSW retains minority ownership stakes in various 
companies, including Ausgrid , Endeavour Energy, and WestConnex, which are 
equity accounted. We consider exposures to these entities to be potential 
contingent liabilities for NSW. 
 
NSW local councils are another potential a source of contingent liability. 
They are established under state legislation, are responsible to the state 
government, and may borrow from TCorp under guarantee from the state. Given 
the low leverage of NSW's local councils, we consider this risk to be 
negligible. 
 
Economy recuperating from bushfires and COVID-19-induced recession; excellent 
financial management and Australia's institutional settings continue to 
support NSW's ratings 
The NSW government expects real GSP growth of around -0.75% in fiscal 2021 and 
+2.5% in fiscal 2022 as it recovers from the COVID-19 recession. State final 
demand lifted 6.8% in the September 2020 quarter. The national economy is also 
starting to recuperate; nationwide GDP grew 3.3% quarter on quarter in 
September 2020, following a steep decline of 7.0% in June 2020. While the 
contraction in the first half of 2020 was historically large, Australia is 
outperforming most other advanced economies. 
 
Australia's states have been successful in suppressing the spread of 
coronavirus--notwithstanding a second wave of infections in the neighboring 
state of Victoria, which was contained by November 2020. NSW has eased most 
physical distancing restrictions. Workplaces, schools, and hospitality venues 
are mostly open. Interstate travel restrictions are also being lifted. 
Australia's international borders are closed, apart from some inbound travel 
permitted from New Zealand, causing damage to NSW's education and tourism 
industries. 
 
Fiscal and monetary policy in Australia are now extremely accommodative. The 
federal government is delivering a large wage-subsidy program and various 
stimulus measures, including accelerated personal income tax cuts. The RBA has 
lowered its policy rate to a historic low of 0.10%. It has also introduced 
forward guidance, a A$100 billion asset purchase program, and a term funding 
facility for the banking system. 
 
The continued easing of restrictions has helped buoy consumer and business 
confidence. NSW's unemployment rate stood at 6.5% as of October 2020, a little 
better than the 7.0% national average. The state has regained about 80% of 
jobs lost at the height of the pandemic. For NSW, the COVID-19 crisis comes 
not long after a prolonged drought and severe bushfires over the 2019-2020 
Australian summer. The latter burnt some 5.5 million hectares and destroyed 
A$900 million in infrastructure. 
 
NSW is the largest subnational economy in Australia, accounting for about 
one-third of national GDP. Its populace is wealthy by international standards, 
with GSP per capita of around US$55,600. Its economy is services-driven and 
highly diversified. NSW has about 8.1 million residents. The state capital, 
Sydney, is Australia's largest city and most important commercial hub. 
 
The NSW government's longstanding focus on control of operating expenses 
contributes to our positive assessment of its financial management. NSW has 
successfully implemented several rounds of savings measures, kept public 
sector wage growth low, and is a global leader in utilizing its balance sheet 
to support its infrastructure strategy. 
 
NSW's Fiscal Responsibility Act 2012 commits the state (at general government 
level) to keeping operating expense growth below long-term average operating 
revenue growth, currently calculated at 5.6% per annum. The state expects to 
breach this target only in fiscal years 2020 and 2021. We note that NSW has 
reanchored its target for fully funding its superannuation liabilities (i.e., 
defined-benefit pension liabilities), delaying the target date to 2040 from 
2030. We think NSW's funding commitment remains credible at this stage, and so 
the change does not weigh on our credit assessment. 
 
Supporting the state's management is the institutional framework within which 
all Australian states and territories operate. We consider this framework to 
be one of the strongest and most predictable for subsovereign governments 
globally. It promotes a robust management culture and high levels of financial 
disclosure and transparency. 
 
The NSW government produces annual budgets that include detailed projections 
for three years beyond the budgeted fiscal year; it also produces midyear 
updates and audited final financial outcomes, generally within four months of 
period-end. Accounts are prepared on both a cash and accrual basis, with 
public corporations consolidated in these accounts. This year, Australia's 
states and territories made a coordinated decision to postpone their usual 
annual budgets to the fourth quarter of 2020 or later.

title: ANALYSIS-New government in New Zealand could spell changes for pioneering  central bank
text:
* Labour, NZ First want to add employment to RBNZ mandate

* That would mark shift for pioneer of inflation-targeting

* NZ First also wants greater currency intervention

By Ana Nicolaci da Costa and Charlotte Greenfield

WELLINGTON, Oct 12 (Reuters) - The formation of a centre-left government in New Zealand after an inconclusive election last month would likely spell big changes for its central bank, the pioneer of the inflation-targeting regime adopted across the world.

The Labour-Green bloc has an even chance with the ruling National Party to form a government, if it can agree to a deal with the nationalist New Zealand First Party after talks this week.

For 28 years, New Zealand's central bank has had the single aim of keeping inflation between a set range. But Labour wants to add employment to the bank's mandate, a goal shared by NZ First which also wants to broaden the Reserve Bank of New Zealand's (RBNZ) focus to include greater management of the local dollar's value against other currencies.

"It's a huge change. We've had over 25 years of an extraordinarily successful monetary policy that has been copied around the world," said Arthur Grimes, RBNZ's chief economist in the early 1990s and Board Chair between 2003 and 2013. Any change without careful consideration and analysis would be "extraordinary", he added.

New Zealand was first to formally grant its central bank independence and first, in 1989, to introduce an official inflation target after grappling with annual price rises as high as 18 percent during the 1980s.

Though its economy is only the world's 53rd largest, New Zealand has earned a reputation for its economic experimentation and free market approach over the past three decades.

Its inflation targeting soon became the global economic orthodoxy.

"I don't think people treated it terribly seriously (at first)," said Ted Truman, a former U.S. Federal Reserve official, who spent a month in New Zealand 16 years ago researching inflation targeting.

"Five or six years later it was much more respected and people flocked to New Zealand to find out how they were doing it... which is why I was there."

Don Brash, who was governor when the inflation target was introduced, said the idea came from a TV interview with Roger Douglas, a Labour finance minister in the 1980s. Douglas was asked if he was happy with a drop in inflation to below 10 percent.

"He said: 'No, I'm looking at price stability like zero to 1 percent' and that was I think the first formulation of the target in numerical terms," Brash told Reuters.

The initial 0-2 percent target was widened in 1996 and then lifted in 2002 to its current 1-3 percent.

New Zealand's per capita income dropped during the radical reforms of the 1980s but has since stabilised. Its employment rate has consistently out-performed other developed countries for the past decade and inflation has remained in check.

DUAL-MANDATE CLUB

Labour has said it is committed to the inflation target but wants to add the goal of full employment, bringing it in line with the likes of Australia and the United States.

Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) Governor Philip Lowe is a fan of his broader mandate which comprises stable inflation, full employment and "economic prosperity".

"It's meant that we've been able to take our time in getting inflation back (to target)," he said recently. "We're prepared to be patient."

Grimes, however, argues that history proves monetary policy cannot have a sustained impact on employment.

"It would be like having someone who is running for health minister argue for a cancer drug to be used for heart issues," said Grimes, who was in close contact with central bank officials from Britain as they moved to inflation targeting.

Analysts say the proposed change could lead to a higher bar for the central bank to raise rates as the RBNZ balances the need to keep inflation in check with that of securing employment growth - a trade off other central banks with dual mandates have had to grapple with.

"I had a conversation with Alan Greenspan once and he expressed envy for the fact that we had a single mandate," Brash said. "He understands full well if the two are in conflict at some point, which one do you give priority to?"

Greenspan did not respond to requests for comment.

POLICY SINGAPORE-STYLE

NZ First also favours greater intervention in the foreign exchange market, with leader Winston Peters even touting a Singapore-style system where a currency target path replaces official interest rates and the central bank intervenes to manage currency swings.

Paul Dales, chief Australia and New Zealand economist at Capital Economics in Sydney said this would represent "a complete shake-up" of New Zealand's monetary policy and was unlikely to materialize.

He said greater central bank intervention was also unlikely given the RBNZ is bound by its "traffic light" system which guides any intervention and that any changes "would be tantamount to political interference in the central bank".

Instead, Labour could agree to make a mention of the exchange rate in the central bank's policy target agreement, along with price stability and full employment.

"If they put something like that in, it would be a rhetorical win for Winston ... it wouldn't necessarily change very much in substance at all," said Michael Reddell, a former RBNZ official.

(Reporting by Ana Nicolaci da Costa and Charlotte Greenfield; Additional reporting by Wayne Cole in Sydney; Editing by Lincoln Feast)

title: Global Equities Roundup: Market Talk
text:
0117 GMT - One of the major talking points around the Australian economy this year has been roaring house prices and rising household debt. It's been key to RBA caution around further rate cuts. That now seems to be fading. The question now is: Will that shift the needle for the RBA, which is also focused on the soft job market? Speculation that the market is moving through its peak phase of growth is likely to be supported by CoreLogic data when April housing market results are published on Monday. The CoreLogic hedonic home value index has virtually held steady over the first 27 days of the month for the five city aggregate index, with a subtle fall in Sydney values over the month to date.(james.glynn@wsj.com; Twitter @JamesGlynnWSJ)

0113- GMT - Malaysian stocks open higher, allowing the FTSE Bursa Malaysia Index to for now top resistance at 1770. It's up 0.2% at 1771 after setting a fresh 23-month closing high Thursday, with electricity utility Tenaga Nasional gaining 1% after its F2Q report and lender CIMB rising 0.9%. Group Holdings. Meanwhile, palm-oil planter Kuala Lumpur Kepong drops 1.1% early. (yantoultra.ngui@wsj.com; @yantoultra)

21:04 ET - The iPhone 7 did little to juice Apple (AAPL) sales last quarter, according to IDC data. The research firm estimates AAPL shipped 51.6 million units in 1Q, versus 51.2 million a year earlier. That's somewhat disappointing for AAPL, which releases a new phone every other year and typically a new model like the iPhone 7 would offer enough new features to drive considerably more growth. AAPL's quarterly report comes Tuesday. (tripp.mickle@wsj.com)

Japanese markets are closed next week for national holidays except Monday and Tuesday. Ahead of that, some electronics stocks which had rallied of late are pulling back as results come in decent but not surprisingly great. Omron slides 8% and Advantest skids 8.7%. The Nikkei is off 0.1% at 19230. (kosaku.narioka@wsj.com)

On the flip side, it's crucial whether the greenback can be well-supported around Y111, yesterday's low. A breakdown would bring Y110 back into play. The dollar is around Y111.30. (hiroyuki.kachi@wsj.com)

That makes China Merchants Bank (3968.HK) a standout as the country's largest non-state-owned lender logged 8.9% earnings growth. While in line with Jefferies' estimate, such growth is the most among sizable Chinese banks. Net interest income rose 1.8% despite a 19-basis-point drop in margin while fee and commission income fell 6%. Shares have rebounded of late to go into today's last session of April roughly flat. (john.wu@wsj.com)

With the currency falling under its own weight of last, the RBA could facilitate that process by signaling in the statement that the door to more interest-rate cuts is slightly more ajar than the market realizes, says Greg McKenna, chief market strategist at AxiTrader. (john.wu@wsj.com)

Mount Gibson's net cash balance is equivalent to A$0.41, yet the stock is at A$0.36. UBS puts Koolan Island's net present value at A$0.12; the mine has been shuttered since a sea wall failed in late 2014. title: Global  Forex  and Fixed Income Roundup: Market Talk
text:
0714 GMT - Denmark's Dong Energy looks poised to focus on additional growth and higher payments to shareholders after improving its credit metrics in 2016, prompting UniCredit to cut its bond recommendation to marketweight from overweight. This change in focus should weaken - or remain stable at best - over the next few years. The bank also cites Dong bonds' outperformance versus the iBoxx universe since early August as a reason behind the recommendation cut. Meanwhile, a downgrade by Moody's could drop Dong's hybrid bonds out of the iBoxx investment grade index. While this is an unlikely scenario, current valuations don't compensate investors enough for the uncertainty, UniCredit adds. (tasos.vossos@wsj.com, @tasosvos)

0711 GMT - Klovern's higher leverage versus peers Kungsleden and FastPartner makes the Swedish firm's bonds prone to underperformance if the real estate market deteriorates, Danske Bank says in a note. This is why it keeps its underweight recommendation on Klovern bonds. Still, Danske likes Klovern's positive operating performance, which continued in 1Q, and expects it to focus on organic growth through development projects. All of Klovern's outstanding bonds are denominated in Swedish krona. (tasos.vossos@wsj.com, @tasosvos)

0710 GMT - The government bond market has one more reason to keep a close eye on Thursday's European Central Bank press conference: possible technical details on the reinvestment of maturing bonds held under the public sector purchase program. Around EUR1 billion of two-year paper bought at the start of the so-called PSPP in early 2015 matured last week, according to Commerzbank calculations. When the PSPP first started, the minimum remaining maturity of eligible assets was set at two years; as of January 2017, it stands at just one year. Unlike the Bank of England, which maintains a certain level of purchased gilts by reinvesting maturing issues, the ECB only has a monthly asset-buying target. (tasos.vossos@wsj.com, @tasosvos)

0708 GMT - Gas-export restrictions planned by Australia to solve a gas shortage are already fuelling perceptions of political risk, says the Australian Petroleum Production and Exploration Association. It warns the government to avoid the interventionist route of Argentina. "Exploration in Australia is at a 30-year low. So the future pipeline of gas that we need to sustain supply into the market is very precarious," says APPEA Chief Executive Malcolm Roberts. "We're very concerned about the signal it sends to investors. There's a lot of uncertainty about what the rules are now in Australia." The industry group insists the solution to high prices and threat of a looming supply shortfall is more gas not more regulation. (rob.taylor@wsj.com; @WSJRobTaylor)

0658 GMT - Moody's views JAB Holding's potential sales of Jimmy Cho and Bally International positively, as cash proceeds can help reduce the investment firm's debt leverage. JAB could raise at least GBP480 million from Jimmy Choo, but Moody's expects "significantly less" from the Bally disposal. Bond holders are yet to show much enthusiasm, as the price of the 2.125% 2022 euro bond remains near its lowest level since June 2016, based on Factset data. (tasos.vossos@wsj.com, @tasosvos)

0647 GMT - ECB President Mario Draghi should be determined to avoid a hawkish surprise in Thursday's press conference, but this is not enough for Commerzbank to change its cautious stance on German government bonds. The German bank mentions 0.4% as a key level: while yields remain below that point, sentiment should be bearish. The 10-year German government bond is trading at 0.36% Thursday morning, based on Tradeweb data. Yields move inversely to bond prices: when one drops, the other one rises. (tasos.vossos@wsj.com, @tasosvos)

0641 GMT - The Swiss National Bank said its first quarter profit was 7.9 billion francs, as higher global equity markets lifted the value of its massive portfolio of foreign assets. The figures tend to have more symbolic value, since the SNB's monetary policies are aimed at keeping inflation under 2%, not at maximizing profits or its share price. (brian.blackstone@wsj.com)

0639 GMT - Switzerland's trade surplus was 2.8 billion francs last month, down slightly from February but still suggesting that Swiss exporters have weathered the effects of the strong Swiss franc. The first quarter surplus was CHF10.8 billion, which should support GDP growth. (brian.blackstone@wsj.com)

0538 GMT - Although the Bank of Japan didn't in any way alter the pace of its annual Japanese government purchases, at some Y80 trillion, it would have been an opportune time for the central bank to change its message regarding its purchasing pace, says Takahiro Sekido, Japan strategist for Bank of Tokyo-Mitsubishi UFJ in a note. There is a gap between its proclaimed pace and actual purchases of Y60 trillion a year, he notes. (suryatapa.bhattacharya@wsj.com)
