title: DJ Australian Equities Roundup -- Market Talk
text:
0045 GMT -- Job advertisements in Australia fell 1.2% in February from a month earlier to the lowest level since October, according to the latest ANZ job ads survey. ANZ's chief economist Warren Hogan says the February fall may reflect some caution on the part of businesses amid heightened financial market volatility and negative news on the global economy. There's also a bit of tricky seasonal adjustment at this time of the year. But even discounting some of the decline, there's still been a slowing in trend growth in job advertising over the past six months, he adds. "While the economy finished 2015 on a relatively strong note, as shown in last week's better-than-expected GDP figures, 2016 is already shaping up as one of conflicting forces," Hogan says. (rachel.pannett@wsj.com; Twitter: @RachelPannett)

0041 GMT -- UBS drops Oz Minerals (OZL.AU) to neutral from buy, citing a full share price and risks around the cost of developing its Carrapateena copper-gold deposit in South Australia state. Oz Minerals recently estimated the project would cost about A$770 million, and once producing would add an estimated A$150 million in average annual cashflow by 2019. The company believes Carrapateena's net present value is more than A$600 million, but UBS thinks this is too bullish. UBS puts the project's NPV at A$530 million using its long-term copper price forecast of US$2.95/lb and AUD/USD of 0.75. "We like Oz Minerals 's current balance sheet strength, 2016-18 cash flow generation and liquidity, but UBS sees copper as one of the more vulnerable commodities to lower prices," UBS says. "While we believe that OZ Minerals has unlocked long-term Carrapateena value, this view hinges on higher copper prices." Still, UBS lifts its price target on Oz Minerals by 12% to A$5.50/share. OZL last traded at A$5.40. (david.winning@wsj.com; Twitter: @dwinningWSJ)

0040 GMT -- Now is not the time for existing investors to bail out of retailers JB Hi-Fi (JBH.AU) and Harvey Norman (HVN.AU), but don't go chasing their shares either, says Morgan Stanley . The broker, which has an 'Equal-weight' call on JB Hi-Fi and an 'Underweight' call on Harvey Norman, says the combined earnings of both stocks are above prior peaks and their share prices look full. However, the tailwind from a strong Australian housing market is likely to continue for a while yet, Morgan Stanley says. As a result, the broker lifts its price target on JB Hi-Fi and Harvey Norman by 4.5% to A$23.00 per share and by 16% to A$4.40/share, respectively. "Given the 6-9 month lag from housing indicators (approvals, prices, auction clearance rates) to retail sales across furniture, bedding, electrical and electronics, we think JB Hi-Fi and Harvey Norman are set for strong growth during FY17," Morgan Stanley says. JBH last traded at A$22.02; HVN last at A$4.69. (david.winning@wsj.com; @dwinningWSJ)

0024 GMT -- The strengthening Australian dollar (it reached an eight-month high of US$0.7443 Friday) will start to put pressure on the Reserve Bank of Australia , and the central bank may look to intervene in the market to devalue the currency, OFX's Adrian Steele says. RBA board member John Edwards told The Wall Street Journal last month he'd be more comfortable with the Australian dollar trading around US$0.65, in the first sign for some time of unease on the central bank board about the level of the Australian dollar. At the time it was trading at US$0.7150. Now, it's at US$0.7414. OFX tips a range of US$0.7350-US$0.7450 today. The rally comes as iron ore--Australia's biggest export--is at its highest level since October. Actual intervention by the RBA is rare, but jawboning is always an option. (rachel.pannett@wsj.com; Twitter: @RachelPannett)

0022 GMT -- Spanish infrastructure firm Ferrovial (FRRVY) has increased its stake in takeover target Broadspectrum (BRS.AU), despite saying recently it was reconsidering its bid when the Australian contractor lost its front-runner status for a key contract. Ferrovial has lifted its stake to 2.09% from 1.01% in mid-February, according to a filing with the Australian Securities Exchange . While the numbers suggest the Spanish company is still interested, they also show it continues to make extremely slow progress ahead of its March 21 deadline, suggesting it will need to sweeten its offer if it's to get a deal over the line, especially given it lacks the backing of some large shareholders and the Broadspectrum board. Sydney-based Broadspectrum rejected Ferrovial's A$1.35/share bid in January, saying it undervalues the company, and a report by Ernst & Young valued Broadspectrum's shares at A$1.71 to A$1.98. (rebecca.thurlow@wsj.com; Twitter: @beckthurlow)

0019 GMT -- Iron-ore producers are racing higher on rising prices for steelmaking commodity. Fortescue Metals (FMG.AU), which relies on iron ore for all its profits and has surprised brokers with the scale of its cost-cutting, is the standout Down Under. Shares in Fortescue have rallied 61% since the start of February to A$2.79/share. The big Anglo-Australian groups BHP Billiton (BHP.AU) and Rio Tinto (RIO.AU) are also benefiting, up 21% and 19%, respectively, over the same period. Spot iron ore trades at a five-month high. (rhiannon.hoyle@wsj.com; Twitter: @RhiannonHoyle)

0001 GMT -- Australia's construction industry contracted for a third-straight month in February, with a private sector index published by Australian Industry Group and the Housing Industry Association slipping 0.2 points to 46.1 (readings below 50 mark a contraction, with the distance from 50 indicating the strength of the decrease). "With housing approvals slipping in recent months, unless we see a period of sustained growth in commercial construction and a pick-up in infrastructure investment, it is unlikely that the construction industry will be a source of growth for the economy or jobs in coming months," Ai Group's head of policy, Peter Burn, says. That's a potential worry for the Reserve Bank of Australia , given that until recently the housing market was one of the few frothy parts of the economy as a long mining investment boom drew to a close. (rachel.pannett@wsj.com; @RachelPannett)

2354 GMT -- This week promises readings on confidence levels in Australia, with NAB 's business survey, due Tuesday, expected to give up a little ground--softening to +1 from +2 in January--according to J.P. Morgan , while Westpac 's consumer sentiment survey Wednesday may hold on to February's surprise strength given recent falls in local gasoline prices and relative stability in equities markets. In terms of the business survey, J.P. Morgan 's analysts say they'll be keeping a close eye on the employment sub-index, which slipped into negative territory last month (from 0 to -1), suggesting momentum in the labor data has slowed into the new year. Turning to consumer sentiment, the correlation between consumer confidence and consumption has faltered in the past few years. Still, households' assessment of their own finances will be important given the likelihood of a further slowing in the local housing market, they say. (rachel.pannett@wsj.com; Twitter: @RachelPannett)

2336 GMT -- Australian biotech CSL (CSL.AU) has received U.S. Food and Drug Administration approval for the use of its Idelvion product in the treatment of haemophilia B. UBS says Idelvion, which offers patients prolonged dosing intervals of up to 14 days, could provide superior treatment at same annual cost, making it a winner with patients, although CSL hasn't disclosed pricing yet. The broker, which has a Buy rating on the stock, expects Idelvion sales in the U.S. to ramp up in stages, reaching US$300 million by fiscal 2019. (rebecca.thurlow@wsj.com; @beckthurlow)

2323 GMT -- UBS ups its price target on Alumina (AWC.AU) by 15% to A$1.50/share, citing a recovery that's underway in alumina prices and good cost control. Although alumina prices fell by 44% on-year to a low of US$198/ton in January, they have since rebounded 15% to US$230/ton due to production cutbacks in China and elsewhere. UBS expects Alumina's 1Q ebitda margin to be US$15/ton, representing the lowest level since 2009. However, at today's spot prices, the ebitda margin more than doubles to US$32/ton. UBS , which keeps a buy call on the stock, says it may have overestimated Alumina's costs and now believes the company's annual cost base to be US$3 billion. "This is below our estimate prior to the results release and is the principal driver of our increase in earnings (+33% in 2017 to US$235 million) and lift in net present value (+16% to A$1.50/share)," UBS says. AWC last traded at A$1.36. (david.winning@wsj.com: @dwinningWSJ)

2313 GMT -- SG Fleet's (SGF.AU) appointment as one of two panelists to provide fleet management services to the New South Wales government could boost its annual net profit by 2%, assuming a 50% win rate, says Macquarie. The NSW government's fleet totals around 22,000 vehicles and management services are to be split between SG Fleet and another Australian-listed company, Smartgroup (SIQ.AU). "We estimate Smartgroup 's average revenue per vehicle in this part of its business is A$550 per annum and SG Fleet's is A$750," Macquarie says. "This implies an annual value for the 22,000 vehicle fleet of A$12 million-A$15 million." Still, Macquarie estimates pricing would be lower than this range, due to the size of the fleet. SGF last traded at A$3.75; SIQ last at A$4.62. (david.winning@wsj.com; @dwinningWSJ)

6 Mar 2016 23:11 ET  DJ Australian Equities Roundup -- Market Talk -2-

2306 GMT -- What is the impact on CSR's (CSR.AU) earnings per share if the building materials supplier completes its up to A$150 million buyback in full? Macquarie estimates it could add 10.8% to FY17 estimates, although it's likely to be a gradual program finishing in March 2018. "In the context of a peaking Australian residential building market, acquiring assets or expanding capacity would have been deemed a poor strategic move," says Macquarie. "A buy-back, conversely, is a wise decision, especially given the depressed valuation of the stock and the lack of franking credits for special dividends." It retains an underperform call, and A$2.60/share price target. CSR last traded at A$3.10. (david.winning@wsj.com: @dwinningWSJ)

2304 GMT -- Macquarie has reshuffled the pack among listed Australian packaging companies in the wake of a positive February earnings season, moving to install Amcor (AMC.AU) as its top stock pick. The broker says a near-term catalyst for Orora (ORA.AU)--namely, M&A--was played out with the recent US$77 million purchase of IntegraColor, a U.S. provider of point-of-purchase retail display marketing. Still, it retains an outperform call on Orora as the company retains more than A$200 million in firepower that it can use, including for additional deals. "Amcor re-affirmed its position as a high quality, well managed business and the Americas is a clear M&A focus moving forward," Macquarie says. "A tighter credit environment should increase its opportunity set." It has an outperform call on Amcor and A$16.00/share price target. AMC last traded at A$13.93; ORA last at A$2.39. (david.winning@wsj.com; @dwinningWSJ)

2253 GMT -- Australian shares are likely to rise in early trade, taking their lead from U.S. stocks which gained Friday on stronger than expected payrolls, while oil and iron ore prices also rose. Market Matters forecasts the ASX 200 to start 38 points higher at 5,128. But the trading advisory firm sees warnings signs in last week's trade suggesting the recent rally may not be sustained. While the ASX/200 rose 4.3% led by surging bank and resources stocks, the healthcare sector struggled to grind out small gains with some stocks in the sector falling. "This price action is what Market Matters would expect if our short term positive view for equities, followed by a significant correction, is to unfold. We are currently witnessing an aggressive rally in the underperforming stocks as opposed to strong buying in the quality names. The recent buying is likely to be a combination of short covering by traders and underweight fund managers chasing a few battered stocks that can be perceived to be cheap." (rebecca.thurlow@wsj.com; @beckthurlow)

2252 GMT -- Building materials supplier CSR's (CSR.AU) planned buyback of shares worth up to A$150 million sends a strong positive signal to the market regarding the outlook, and its capacity to generate sufficient cash flow to meet its asbestos liability and fund growth, says Credit Suisse . CSR expects the share-buyback program to start on March 21 and continue through March, 2018. "While the buyback does not come as a surprise, we understood management preferred a growth and diversification strategy away from aluminum, which should invariably be accompanied by a higher stock rating," Credit Suisse says. "For now, we expect the buyback to support the share price and stem the material underperformance (aluminum-led) over the past 12 months." The broker retains a neutral call and A$3.20/share price target. CSR last traded at A$3.10. (david.winning@wsj.com: @dwinningWSJ)

2235 GMT -- Bell Potter lifts its earnings forecasts and price target for SG Fleet (SGF.AU), after it was appointed as one of two panelists to provide fleet management services to the New South Wales government. The appointment represents a 22,000-vehicle opportunity split between SG Fleet and another Australian-listed company, Smartgroup (SIQ.AU), Bell Potter says. "Given the uncertainty around the level of work that SG Fleet will win, as well as our existing fleet growth assumptions, we have chosen to increase our forecast fleet size in FY17 by 5,000 vehicles," says Bell Potter, which rates SG Fleet at buy. "The contract is for fleet management only; therefore SG Fleet will be mainly generating management and maintenance income initially with further income streams to follow as the fleet turns over." Bell Potter raises its F17 and FY18 EPS forecasts by 2.3% and 0.8%, respectively. Its price target goes to A$4.25/share, from A$4.20/share before. SGF last traded at A$3.66. (david.winning@wsj.com: @dwinningWSJ)

2232 GMT -- Currency strategists are hoping for new clues that the Australian central bank may consider further interest-rate cuts, after the Australian dollar rose to US$0.7443 over the weekend--the highest level in about eight months. title: Australian Dollar up Late as Commodity Prices Rally
text:
SYDNEY--The Australian dollar maintained its recent strength on Monday as stronger commodity prices offset a weaker growth outlook for China, the biggest buyer of the resource-rich nation's exports.

At 0425 GMT, the Australian dollar was trading at US$0.7417, up from US$0.7355 at a similar time in local trading on Friday. It traded at an eight-month high of US$0.7443 in New York on Friday.

Currency strategists are hoping for new clues that the Australian central bank may consider further interest-rate cuts to tame the rising currency.

Philip Lowe, the Deputy Governor of the Reserve Bank of Australia, might provide fresh views on the strengthening currency, when he speaks at an industry congress in Adelaide on Tuesday at 2320 GMT.

"Will he offer an opinion on what he thinks of [the Australian dollar] knocking on the door of US$0.75?" said Ray Attrill, global co-head of currency strategy at National Australia Bank. He said a jump in iron-ore prices and a weaker-than-expected U.S. data on hourly-wage growth boosted the Aussie dollar over the weekend. Iron ore--Australia's biggest export--is at its highest level since October.

RBA board member John Edwards told The Wall Street Journal last month he would be more comfortable with the Australian dollar trading around US$0.65, in the first sign for some time of unease on the central bank board about the level of the Australian dollar. At the time it was trading at US$0.7150.

"The strengthening Australian dollar will start to put pressure on the Reserve Bank of Australia and they may look to intervene in the market to devalue the currency," OFX's Adrian Steele said in a note. Actual intervention by the RBA is rare, but jaw boning in an attempt to talk down a stubbornly high currency is a familiar practice to traders.

The Australian dollar could also further strengthen against the New Zealand dollar, as the Reserve Bank of New Zealand may start to jawbone its currency at its next interest-rate decision Thursday, said Kay Van-Petersen, a global macro strategist at Saxo Capital Markets in Singapore. The Kiwi has soared nearly 5% since the start of February, prompting Mr. Van-Petersen to enter a tactical long bet on the Aussie dollar against its New Zealand counterpart ahead of the RBNZ meeting.

On the data front, this week promises readings on confidence levels in Australia, with NAB's business survey, due Tuesday, expected to give up a little ground--softening to +1 from +2 in January--according to J.P. Morgan, while Westpac's consumer sentiment survey Wednesday may hold on to February's surprise strength given recent falls in local gasoline prices and relative stability in equities markets.

-- Vera Sprothen in Sydney contributed to this article

title: RPT- FOREX -Yen weakens on talk of Japanese snap election
text:
(Repeats to more subscribers)

* Yen sags as Nikkei rises on renewed election speculation

* RBA's Kent: intervention to weaken Aussie remains an option

* Swiss franc hits two-year highs, eyes on SNB cap (Updates with Fed's Dudley, details)

By Anirban Nag

LONDON, Nov 13 (Reuters) - The dollar rose towards a recent seven-year high against the yen on Thursday, driven by renewed speculation that Japanese Prime Minister Shinzo Abe will call a snap election in December.

The dollar's rise, though, slowed in the European session after New York Federal Reserve President William Dudley said any premature tightening in monetary policy could hurt economic recovery.

The dollar was up 0.2 percent at 115.65 yen, not far from the seven-year high of 116.11 yen struck on Tuesday. The euro too rose 0.4 percent to 144.15 yen while the high-yielding New Zealand dollar hit a seven-year high against the yen as the Japanese currency continued to cede ground.

An election is seen returning Abe to power with a bigger mandate, which analysts believe would allow him to implement a second round of reflationary policies and possibly delay a planned sales tax hike. That has spurred a rally in Japanese stocks and weighed on the yen.

"Dollar/yen is headed higher and all those who missed the bus at lower levels will use the political developments to build long dollar positions," said Geoff Yu, strategist at UBS.

A senior figure in Abe's ruling party told reporters it appeared the premier had decided to call an election. Abe is expected to make his decision depending on the strength of economic indicators, with third-quarter gross domestic product data due on Monday.

The market was also awaiting U.S. jobless claims data on Thursday and retail sales on Friday. Those numbers may reinforce perceptions that the U.S. economy is doing better than Europe or Japan, helping to push the dollar higher against the euro and the yen.

The Australian dollar fell after an official at the Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) said it had not ruled out intervening to sell the currency, which it views as overvalued. The Aussie recovered later to trade at $0.8745, but traders were cautious.

"If the general dollar strength does not ensure that the Australian dollar is capped then the RBA will no doubt do so," said Thu Lan Nguyen, a currency strategist at Commerzbank.

The Swiss franc also remained on intervention watch.

The franc has hit two-year highs against the euro this week as traders positioned for a Nov. 30 referendum on whether the central bank should be required to hold at least 20 percent of its assets in gold, although polls show voters are likely to vote against the proposal.

The Swiss National Bank has said that a 'Yes' vote would limit the central bank's ability to maintain a stable currency.

The franc hit a new two-year high of 1.20175 francs per euro on Thursday, not far from the cap of 1.20 francs that the SNB imposed more than three years ago.

Vice Chairman Jean-Pierre Danthine said on Thursday that the cap would be in place for the foreseeable future. (Editing by John Stonestreet and Susan Fenton)

title: Australia  cenbank says A$  intervention  remains an option
text:
SYDNEY, Nov 13 (Reuters) - A top Australian central banker on Thursday repeated that intervention to lower the Australian dollar remained an option, though he showed no sign it was being considered in any way.

Answering questions after giving a speech in Sydney, Assistant Governor Christopher Kent was asked if intervention had been ruled out. He noted that RBA Governor Glenn Stevens had stated in the past that intervention was an option and that it would not be sensible to rule it out completely.

The central bank has consistently said there would be a very high bar for intervention and has not undertaken any action in currency markets in recent years.

The mere mention of intervention did knock the local dollar down briefly, but it soon recovered to above 87 U.S. cents . (Reporting by Wayne Cole; Editing by Shri Navaratnam)

title: Australian Dollar Down After Strong U.S. Housing Report
text:
SYDNEY--The Australian dollar was lower Wednesday in line with gains by the greenback on news overnight of a jump in U.S. housing construction.

U.S. home builders broke ground on 101,000 new projects in July, for a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 1.093 million units, according to the Commerce Department. That is a 16% improvement over June's housing starts.

The impressive numbers indicate that housing recovery is still on solid ground. That was thrown into doubt earlier this year by a plunge in housing starts. The decline took January's starts down to where they were a year earlier.

At 0530 GMT Wednesday the Australian dollar was around US$0.9293 compared with US$0.9331 late Tuesday.

The Aussie remained relatively well supported in the Asian trading session despite comments by Reserve Bank of Australia governor Glenn Stevens that intervention to sell the currency remains "on the table" as a policy option.

In a testimony before parliament, Stevens said intervention is most effective when not telegraphed to the markets, admitting the issue was under serious consideration when the currency was higher in 2013.

Still, Stevens gave no impression that the central bank is on the verge of cutting interest rates, stating that at a record low of 2.5%, interest rates were doing enough to support the economy, and further stimulus must come from elsewhere.

The comments prompted Goldman Sachs to abandon their forecast of a September interest rate cut, saying the next move will be higher in late 2015.

Stevens also said that interest rate increases had not been considered lately.

"Recent RBA commentary confirms that the Bank is comfortably on hold," NAB said in a note to clients.

title: RBA Keeps  Currency Intervention  as Option
text:
SYDNEY--Australia's central bank Gov. Glenn Stevens said intervention in currency markets to help drive the Aussie dollar lower remained a real option.

Speaking to a parliamentary committee Wednesday, Mr. Stevens also said that the chance of a significant drop in the Australian dollar remained under appreciated.

Both remarks are familiar to traders, who tend to interpret them as part of attempts to talk the stubbornly high currency lower.

Australian dollar strength is hurting exporters, especially manufacturers, at a time when the reserve bank is trying to lift the economy, which has been slowing as a long mining-investment boom cools.

Mr. Stevens said direct currency-market intervention remained part of the Reserve Bank of Australia's "toolkit" and was "on the table," adding that the measure would work best if it wasn't telegraphed ahead of time to financial markets.

The currency didn't move significantly on the governor's remarks.

The moment the U.S. Federal Reserve begins to raise interest rates, it is hard to see a scenario in which the Australian dollar would continue rising, Mr. Stevens said.

Despite some weakness in the Australian dollar over the last 18 months, the bank still considers it to be overvalued and a major impediment to growth.

Recently, the central bank cut its estimates for both growth and inflation, forecasting that unemployment, already at the highest level in more than a decade, would remain elevated for some time.

The Australian dollar has continued to trade well above US$0.9000 despite sharp falls in key commodity prices since the start of the year--including iron ore, the country's largest export.

Mr. Stevens said foreign capital flows to Australia, which is often considered a haven, have been a big cause of Aussie dollar strength. He described it as a wall of money entering the country.

Australia is one of only a handful of countries with a AAA sovereign-credit rating, making it relatively attractive to foreign investors. Bond-market yields are also appealing when compared with near-zero interest rates in many developed economies.

The Australian dollar continued to trade around US$0.9300 during the testimony.

Earlier, Mr. Stevens said he remained hopeful that record-low interest rates--at 2.5% for a year now--would eventually spur the economy, which while notching up growth for more than 22 years straight has been losing steam for at least the past couple of years.

"The sorts of forecasts we are setting out at the moment will very likely prove to be conservative," Mr. Stevens said in his testimony. "The frustrating thing is that no one can say when that will happen, or just what might be the proximate trigger."

title: Australia dollar shines after upbeat data, NZ dollar struggles
text:
* Aussie up 0.5 pct vs USD, kiwi & GBP

* China trade numbers, upbeat Australia jobs growth boost AUD

* NZD hurt by RBNZ intervention threat

By Cecile Lefort and Naomi Tajitsu

SYDNEY/WELLINGTON, May 8 (Reuters) - The Australian dollar received a fillip on Thursday from upbeat data in Australia and China, while the New Zealand dollar still nursed losses following a threat of intervention by the Reserve Bank of New Zealand.

The Aussie rose half a cent to $0.9374, though it faces tough resistance at $0.9400, the 76.4 percent retracement of the April-May fall. It was pulling closer to this year's peak of $0.9461, having gained 5 percent since Jan. 1.

The move higher came after China's trade numbers beat expectations, with exports rising 0.9 percent on the year in April. Imports from Australia grew almost 18 percent in April from a year earlier.

The Aussie had already received a leg up on a solid labour report at home. Australian jobs growth outpaced expectations for a third month running in April and helped keep the jobless rate from rising.

The outcome will be welcomed by the Reserve Bank of Australia, which again kept rates on hold this week in expectation that past cuts were working to reenergise the economy.

The futures market <0#YIB:> dipped a touch as it had already priced out any chance of another easing, while swap markets slightly increased the chance that the next move in rates would be up, albeit not until 2015.

"The market is probably a little too complacent on how long they expect the cash rate to remain unchanged. They don't have a full hike priced until September of next year," said Su-Lin Ong, an economist at RBC Capital Markets.

The Aussie rallied across the board and showed the largest increase against its kiwi neighbour. It jumped 0.5 percent to NZ$1.0821, well above a one-month low of NZ$1.0642 touched on Tuesday.

Against the U.S. dollar, the New Zealand dollar was stuck at $0.8654. Investors dumped the currency on Wednesday when the Reserve Bank of New Zealand warned that a historically strong currency could slow the pace of future interest rate rises.

In a speech, RBNZ Graeme Wheeler had also put the possibility of kiwi-selling intervention on the table if economic fundamentals no longer justify currency strength. His comments pushed the kiwi down 0.9 percent, its biggest daily fall since late January.

Broad selling knocked the kiwi down to its lowest in roughly a week against the euro. As a result, the kiwi fell to 80.08 versus a currency basket, retreating from 81.00 on Wednesday, when it matched a post-float high.

Most economists still expect the RBNZ to raise rates to 3.25 percent in June, but analysts said that risks were growing that the central bank may then pause its tightening cycle if the kiwi stays strong.

"It's nice to see some domestic factors emerging in the kiwi pricing, but the ultimate driver is going to be the U.S. dollar," ANZ currency strategist Sam Tuck said.

"We'd expect to see decent demand below $0.8600."

New Zealand government bonds rose, pushing yields 3 basis points lower at the long end of the curve.

Australian government bond futures retreated from multimonth highs, with the three-year bond contract down 3 ticks at 97.120. The 10-year contract was steady at 95.880, having touched a seven-month high of 96.190.   (Editing by Chris Gallagher)

Sentiment was further boosted by the European Central Bank's decision to hold off on any further stimulus measures, which provides some reasurance for the international growth outlook. The S&P/ASX 200 is up 0.6% at 5161.5, with energy and mining stocks supporting gains as BHP Billiton (BHP.AU)rises 1.6% and Rio Tinto (RIO.AU) adds 0.8%. Banks are also higher, with Westpac (WBC.AU) up 1.7% and ANZ Banking (ANZ.AU) up 0.7%. Mr. Spooner says he expects the release Friday of the central bank's policy statement could provide insight into the nuances of its shift to neutral, while any changes to forecasts for inflation and economic growth may give clues on the bank's thinking on the next move for interest rates. (robb.stewart@wsj.com)

Sony said it now expects to lose Y110 billion in the full year through March--reversing a previously forecast profit of Y30 billion--and its second downward revision in just three months. It also said it would sell its struggling PC business, and that it will split off its TV business and operate it as a subsidiary. "It's hard to say how much of the restructuring plan had been factored into prices; everybody knows how challenged the firm is in its electronics business," says David Rubenstein, tech analyst at Advanced Research Japan. "But the forecast cut was large enough to warrant alarm, especially as its rivals appear to be making progress with cutting off money-losing units." Premarket bid/ask levels are at Y1,590/Y1,591 vs Thursday's close at Y1,624. (bradford.frischkorn@wsj.com)

title: Beijing And Bernanke Cut Aussie -- Heard On The Street
text:
(FROM THE WALL STREET JOURNAL 1/4/14) 
   By Rebecca Thurlow 

[Financial Analysis and Commentary]

The Australian dollar has taken a tumble the past few months. There is good reason to think it has further to fall.

The Reserve Bank of Australia has jawboned its currency lower with warnings it might make a rare jump into foreign-exchange markets to boost the flagging economy. But foreign forces are likely to do more to weaken the "Aussie."

The world's fifth-most traded currency and a proxy for China's commodities appetite remains high historically, buying 89 U.S. cents versus US$1.05 a year ago. That's hampering Australia's economy, especially manufacturing and tourism, which otherwise could take up slack from a fading mining boom as China slows.

The Aussie has fallen 6% against the U.S. dollar since October. Besides Reserve Bank of Australia governor Glenn Stevens warning of possible intervention, larger forces help. A central-bank index of Australia's major commodity exports fell in December to its lowest level in more than 3 1/2 years. There are few signs of this reversing, with Chinese manufacturing losing momentum.

Meanwhile, despite the Federal Reserve' curbing its bond-buying and Australian policy rates being near historic lows, the spread between U.S. and Australian bond yields hasn't shrunk much. That should narrow as the central banks move in opposite directions, making the Aussie less attractive.

Mr. Stevens has labeled a level above A$0.90 as unsustainable -- seemingly, a line in the sand. Even a slight bump could prompt action. But as Japan discovered, a more effective way to a weaker currency is loosening monetary policy more broadly. With the central bank's policy rate at 2.5%, Australia has room to cut but worries about pumping up a bubbly housing market. For now, though, it can take it easy and let a slowing China and a tapering Fed do the hard work.

title: Australian Dollar Slides on RBA Comments
text:
SYDNEY--The Australian dollar slumped to its lowest levels in three months Friday, following comments by the country's central bank governor, making it the worst performing top-10 currency globally in the last 24 hours.

Reserve Bank of Australia Gov. Glenn Stevens told the Australian Financial Review in an interview, published Friday that the currency made a lot more sense trading in the mid US$0.85 cent region, rather than US$0.95.

Mr. Stevens said he would prefer to see stimulus delivered to the sluggish economy through a lower currency, rather than through further cuts to interest rates, which are already at record lows.

"To the extent that we get some more easing in financial conditions, at this point it's probably more preferable for that to be via a low currency at the margin than lower interest rates," Mr. Stevens said.

"I thought US$0.85 would be closer to the mark than US$0.95," he said.

At 2:45 a.m. GMT the Australian dollar was trading around US$0.89 compared with US$0.90 at the same time on Thursday.

Mr. Stevens has been talking down the Australian dollar in recent months, with some success. He said recently he was open to the idea of intervention in the currency market to push the Aussie lower.

Prime Minister Tony Abbott also told parliament Thursday there was scope for the Reserve Bank of Australia to consider "prudent" intervention to seek the "best possible level" for the nation.

The government had increased the working capital for the RBA in October by US$7.92 billion, which could be used to weaken the Australian dollar, if the RBA chose to do so.

"Comments from the governor to the media this week continue an ongoing, concerted RBA campaign to 'jawbone' the Australian dollar lower," said Paul Bloxham, chief economist at HSBC, Australia, based in Sydney.

"While it is clearly not the only factor at play, it is arguably having some impact, with the Australian dollar trading at a three month low," he said.

The Reserve Bank of Australia has been trying to spur weaker parts of the economy such as manufacturing and consumer sentiment by cutting interest rates eight times since late 2011. But so far the economy is stuck in low gear, with only tentative signs of a transition away from mining-dependent growth.

The urgency to achieve a lower dollar comes as consumer confidence has fallen, and unemployment has increased. Australia's jobless rate rose to 5.8% in November from 5.7% in October.

The slide in the Australian dollar has come despite news of strong trade data in China at the start of this week and data showing that lending for investment in local housing increased by 8.2% in October.

Diana Mousina, economist at the Commonwealth Bank of Australia said the focus in currency markets has shifted back to the domestic picture.

"A lower Australian dollar and weaker local share market over the month, coupled with a soft third quarter GDP print has dampened expectations around economic performance," she said.

Selling of the Australian dollar against the New Zealand dollar has also added extra weight to the currency's downward slide. The Reserve Bank of New Zealand signaled Thursday it is likely to be one of the central banks in the world to start raising interest rates in 2014.

The glum Australian picture has led markets to increase bets on the likelihood of a further cut in interest rates by the RBA in mid-2014.

Bets that the U.S. Federal Reserve will begin scaling back its monthly bond buying program soon is also weighing on the Australian dollar.

"The fall in the Australian dollar corresponds with global moves, pricing in an improving chance the Fed will begin to scale back its bond buying program next week," said Rob Henderson, head of Australian Economics, Markets at the National Australia Bank.

SYDNEY--The Australian dollar was higher late Tuesday after comments by a senior central bank official that appeared to temper growing expectations of currency market intervention.

Philip Lowe, deputy governor of the Reserve Bank of Australia, said the central bank doesn't rule intervention in or out, but that the threshold for intervening was "fairly high."

The Aussie rose by close to a third of a U.S. cent to just above US$0.9200 after Mr. Lowe's remarks, which he made in response to questions at a business event.

Toward the end of last week, the currency dropped sharply after central bank Governor Glenn Stevens said he was "open minded" on the question of intervention--triggering speculation direct action to drive the currency lower is being considered.

At 0650 GMT, the Australian dollar was trading at US$0.9183, up from US$0.9123 at the same time Monday.

Lowe also forecast the Australian dollar will fall over the medium term in line with falling business investment and an eventual recovery in the U.S. economy.

"While the central bank would like a lower Australian dollar, the likelihood of intervention at this stage is still very low given the bank's preference towards a more natural adjustment through market forces," said David de Ferranti, market analyst at FXCM.

Later in the day, a member of the RBA board, which sets interest rates, said the Australian dollar needs to fall.

"The [Australian] dollar is high...it would be very helpful if it came back a little further than where it is now," said businessman Roger Corbett.

"But certainly the high degree of monetary stimulation in America makes it much harder to get that dollar down," he told The Wall Street Journal.

The International Monetary Fund in a report last week said the Australian dollar was as much as 10% overvalued and, along with a soft labor market and uncertainty in areas outside mining, would continue to act as a headwind on overall economic growth.

Mr. Corbett declined to comment on the possibility of intervention by the central bank on the exchange rate,

"We are entering a period where investment in the resource sector is starting to ease off and it is really important to Australia that we do get a stimulus in the non-resource sector of investment, and that will really come from the consumer," Mr. Corbett said.

"We want to see a higher level of consumer demand in Australia and I think we are starting to see that," he said, adding he remained optimistic about the prospects for the country's economy.

MELBOURNE, Australia--Australian equities logged a third straight daily gain on Tuesday, edging marginally higher thanks to buying of bank shares.

The local market got off to a sluggish start after the Dow Jones Industrial Average edged higher to a fresh record and the Nasdaq Composite Index breached 4000 for the first time in 13 years but failed to hold the level. There was little major corporate news or economic data for investors to latch on to, although the Australian dollar did pick up after Phillip Lowe, deputy governor of the Reserve Bank of Australia, dampened speculation that exchange rate intervention might be imminent.

High-yielding banks were stronger, with Australia & New Zealand Banking, Commonwealth Bank, National Australia Bank and Westpac, between 0.5% and 0.9% higher for the day.

"Time and time again we see local investors taking advantage of any price pullbacks in the major banks and topping up, so to speak," said Stan Shamu, market strategist at IG in Melbourne.

Mr. Shamu said some major resources shares, however, prevented the wider market from extending gains.

title: Central Bankers Try to Square Low Inflation and Asset Bubbles -- Macro Horizons
text:
Macro Horizons covers the main macroeconomic and policy news events affecting foreign-exchange, fixed income and equity markets around the world, as selected by editors in New York, London and Hong Kong. 


 
   By Alen Mattich, Michael Casey, Colin Ng and Michael Arnold 
 

WRAP: Central banks are struggling with pressures pulling them in different directions. Inflation is falling and growth is subdued but asset prices are becoming bubbly. Members of the Bank of Japan's policy committee are questioning whether the country can achieve 2% inflation in its two-year time horizon. The Reserve Bank of Australia is struggling with an overvalued currency that threatens to crush the country's manufacturing sector without cutting rates that would inflate its bubbly housing market even further. And the Bank of England is looking for additional macro-prudential powers it might use to limit bank leverage as the U.K.'s own property market heats up. (AM)

Now it's against the current prime minister, his sister Yingluck Shinawatra. Thailand's protests aren't just Thailand's problem, though. Not that Thailand has the sort of large-scale systemic significance of, say, Iran. But the tension between rich and poor behind the country's on-again, off-again political turbulence isn't unique. Thailand could well show us where other countries are heading, especially in an era when wealthy minorities are made ever richer, while the majority see their real incomes stagnate. (AM)

AUSTRALIA: Australia's central bank sought to dampen speculation that it might intervene to knock down the value of its currency. Days after Reserve Bank of Australia Gov. Tempering of expectations that the central bank might intervene in the currency markets boosted the Australian dollar. The RBA is famously anti-interventionist and last entered the market in October 2008, when the Aussie plunged in the wake of the Lehman Brothers collapse. http://blogs.wsj.com/economics/2013/11/26/boj-beat-minutes-show-split-among-policy-board/

The BOJ has kept policy steady since Gov. Kuroda began his term last April with a shock-and-awe dose of quantitative easing, but beneath the surface, tensions are brewing over the bank's push for 2% inflation. There's growing skepticism inside and out of the BOJ that the target can be met within the promised two-year time horizon, not least because Japan has been fighting falling prices for the better part of two decades, leaving deeply ingrained consumer patterns. Adding to the bank's challenge is an impending sales tax hike next April, which could chill the nascent recovery now underway. (MA)

Central banks have been accused of inflating bubbles again. Indeed, one argument is that bubbles are the only way central banks can maintain full employment given developed economies' secular stagnation. To lean against incipient bubbles, they need additional tools, like being able to constrain how leveraged the economy becomes. Which is what Mr. Carney is calling for. title: ASIA MARKETS: Asia Stocks Mostly Lower; Japan Pulls Back After Rally
text:
Japanese stocks fell on Tuesday, failing to hit a new high for the year, while the Australian dollar picked up after the Reserve Bank of Australia dampened speculation that it's close to intervening in the currency markets.

After bumping up 1.6% over the previous three sessions, the dollar retreated from the recent highs against the yen . Having climbed as high as Yen101.92 on Monday -- its highest level since May -- the greenback eased to Yen101.52 after a strong run that had seen it gain for 9 of the past 12 sessions.

That weakening trend for the yen resulted in substantial gains for Japanese stocks, which also suffered a setback on Tuesday, with the Nikkei Average down 0.7% at 15,515.24. The market closed on Monday just a slither away from a new high for the year, but remains up 8.4% month-to-date.

"The dollar's levels are key to predicting the Nikkei, but even the smallest pause in the yen-weakening trend we've seen will invite profit-taking after the Nikkei's recent run-up," said Kenichi Hirano, market analyst at Tachibana Securities.

Exporters that outperformed the broader market on Monday pulled back on Tuesday due to the stronger currency. Olympus Corp. lost 0.6%, and Tokyo Electron fell 0.7%.

Also in Tokyo, GS Yuasa fell 1.2% after Credit Suisse revised down its rating for the battery maker to underperform from neutral. Fujifilm Holdings jumped 4.3% higher after a Nikkei report said that the company will create cancer treatments jointly with one of the world's leading cancer hospitals, MD Anderson Cancer Center in the U.S.

More broadly, stocks across the region moved lower following an uneventful session on Wall Street. Australia's S&P/ASX 200 rose 0.1%, and South Korea's Kospi added 0.3%.

Stocks in China were steady, with Hong Kong's Hang Seng Index ending flat and the Shanghai Composite down 0.1% on the mainland.

Although stocks in Sydney were little moved, there was some movement in the local currency. The Australian dollar rose back to 92 U.S. cents after Reserve Bank of Australia Deputy Gov. Phillip Lowe said that the threshold for the central bank intervening in the currency market was "fairly high."

Talk of possible intervention by RBA Gov. Glenn Stevens last week, along with slowing growth in Chinese manufacturing activity, has weighed on the Aussie in recent sessions. By early Tuesday afternoon, the currency was at 91.90 U.S. cents.

title: New Zealand Dollar Higher Late as Market Ponders Possible January Rate Hike
text:
WELLINGTON, New Zealand--The New Zealand dollar was trading higher against the U.S. dollar late Tuesday, bolstered by the possibility that the nation's central bank could raise interest rates as early as January.

In late Wellington trading, the New Zealand dollar was at US$0.8254 versus US$0.8224 late Monday. It was at A$0.8978 compared with A$0.8979.

A January rate hike "might seem like blasphemy to some, but we think the case is building," ANZ Chief Economist Cameron Bagrie said.

ANZ's Senior FX manager Sam Tuck said the idea had lent the kiwi some support over the session.

"We have had a bit of an increased focus on when the RBNZ could potentially increase their interest rates...that has sort of fed through into the currency markets," said Mr. Tuck. "The New Zealand economic story continues to grow very strongly," he added.

The central bank has kept interest rates at a record-low 2.5% since March 2011. Most economists are expecting the first rate hike in March next year.

The Kiwi also benefited when the Australian dollar moved higher after Phillip Lowe, deputy governor of the Reserve Bank of Australia, said the threshold for the central bank intervening in the currency market was "fairly high."

Talk of possible intervention by RBA Governor Glenn Stevens last week, along with slowing growth in Chinese manufacturing activity, has weighed on the Aussie in recent sessions.

Mr. Tuck noted, however, that the Kiwi remains strong against the Australian dollar.

"Mostly it's a New Zealand story that's driving the New Zealand dollar, and you can see that by where it is relative to the Australian dollar," said Mr. Tuck.

RBS Senior FX Strategist Greg Gibbs said the Australian dollar is "bouncing in a corrective fashion after its rapid down-move last week with a lack of new catalysts to drive it lower." He said investors will be watching for New Zealand data, including trade data, for direction. However, "the market has a more bearish frame of mind for the Australian dollar."

text:
* Net short positions in yen climb to 6-year high in latest data

* AUD also under pressure, still pressured by RBA intervention talk

* Asian markets monitor China/Japan tensions, Iran developments

By Lisa Twaronite and Ian Chua

TOKYO/SYDNEY, Nov 25 (Reuters) - The dollar rose to a six-month high and the euro pushed to a new four-year peak against the yen in Asian trading on Monday, as investors positioned for yen weakness after speculators had bet on further yen declines.

Positioning data last week showed currency speculators increased net short positions in the Japanese currency to the most in six years, reflecting a belief the Bank of Japan will stay the most aggressive in maintaining its massive stimulus program among major central banks.

"Stops were triggered in dollar/yen, which triggered stops in euro/yen," said Bart Wakabayashi, head of forex at State Street Global Markets in Tokyo.

"It does seem a bit overdone," he said, with no specific macroeconomic move to which the jump can be attributed.

Market participants cited the reluctance of some investors to be short dollars ahead of this week's U.S. Thanksgiving holiday on Thursday. Demand was also seen from Japanese importers, as Monday was a "gotobi" date, or a multiple of five on which books are traditionally settled throughout a month.

The euro rose as far as 137.93 yen, its highest since October 2009, and was last up 0.5 percent at 137.89 yen.

The dollar was up 0.7 percent to 101.87 yen after climbing as high as 101.895 yen on the EBS trading platform, barrelling through the July 8 peak of 101.54 yen to its highest level since May 29.

Against the dollar, the euro slipped 0.1 percent to $1.3540 .

European Central Bank Executive board member Benoit Coeure said on Monday on a visit to Tokyo that slowing price growth, or disinflation, in Europe is likely to continue for now, but will not progress to deflation because the economy is recovering and inflation expectations remain anchored at around 2 percent.

ECB Governing Council member Christian Noyer also said on Monday said that European financial markets are stabilising and interest rates are returning to normal levels.

The euro remains above last week's lows hit after a media report suggested the ECB could lower its deposit rate to negative. The report, which had since been played down by the ECB, sent the euro spiralling to a low of $1.3399 from $1.3584.

The Australian dollar retraced Friday's 2-1/2 month low of $0.9139 according to Reuters data, and was last at $0.9144, down about 0.2 percent on the day and still pressured by the threat of intervention from Reserve Bank of Australia Governor Glenn Stevens.

Stevens last Thursday said the central bank was "open-minded" about intervention to weaken the currency, having consistently argued the Aussie dollar was overvalued compared with fundamentals.

The Aussie slid 2.1 percent last week. Immediate support is seen around $0.9097, the 76.4 percent retracement of its August to October rally.

Traders said the commodity currency could continue to struggle particularly if tensions between China and Japan grew.

China at the weekend suddenly imposed new rules on airspace over islands at the heart of a territorial dispute with Tokyo, prompting Japan and ally the United States to warn of an escalation into the "unexpected" if Beijing enforces the rules.

However, news of a breakthrough that curbed Iran's nuclear activity could help offset any potential fallout from renewed China/Japan tension.

Iran and six world powers clinched a deal on Sunday to curb the Iranian nuclear programme in exchange for initial sanctions relief.

title: Australia Shares End Week on High Note Following U.S. Lead
text:
By Robb M. Stewart

MELBOURNE, Australia--Australian equities rebounded Friday in the wake of a surge on Wall Street as recent worries about when the Federal Reserve will begin trimming its monetary stimulus measures gave way to positive economic news.

A push by the Dow Jones Industrial Average above 16,000 points for the first time set the tone for markets across Asia after Janet Yellen, widely recognized as a dove unlikely to change monetary policy at the Fed, moved a step closer to taking over the top job at the central bank. That followed strong U.S. jobs and manufacturing data that suggests the economic recovery in the U.S. still has traction.

The local benchmark index rose strongly through the course of the session, trimming the week's loss to 1.2%--still the sharpest decline in one and a half months.

"Cyclical names have finished the week on a strong note with industrials leading," said Stan Shamu, a market strategist at IG in Melbourne. "Mining services companies had been a major drag on industrials for most of the week, but have really come to life today."

The local currency remained under pressure, having hit a two-month low late Thursday against the U.S. dollar after the governor of the Reserve Bank of Australia's governor said he remained open to intervention on the exchange rate. Traders have interpreted the comments as further jawboning from central bankers keen to push down a strong Australian dollar that has crimped exporters and added to local costs for mining companies.

The S&P/ASX 200 finished Friday 0.9% higher at 5335.9, the first daily rise of the week.

"Share markets were under pressure again from 'taper' talk over the last week, which resulted in a somewhat volatile ride," said Shane Oliver, head of investment strategy at AMP Capital.

"This is likely just a pause ahead of the resumption of the rising trend as valuations are reasonable, monetary conditions are set to remain very easy and profits are likely to improve next year as global and Australian growth picks up," Mr. Oliver said, adding the benchmark index remained on track to hit 5500 or even higher by year end.

Mining services companies that were weak earlier in the week following a profit warning from WorleyParsons recovered, with Monadelphous Group up 3.5%, Ausdrill up 4.2% and WorleyParsons up 1.8%.

Big mining companies also gained, with BHP Billiton and Rio Tinto both gaining 0.7% after the chairmen of both in separate speeches in recent days said they remain confident China will continue to drive commodities demand.

Shares in the country's four big banks all rose, with Commonwealth Bank up 0.5% and Australia & New Zealand Banking, National Australia Bank and Westpac up 0.7%. The four are still down an average 1.5% for the week.

title: RPT- Australia central bank  open-minded on A$  intervention
text:
(Repeats story first published late on Thursday; no change to text)

SYDNEY, Nov 21 (Reuters) - Australia's top central banker on Thursday said he was "open-minded" on whether to intervene to try and push the Australian dollar lower, escalating a rhetorical campaign against the painfully high currency.

Reserve Bank of Australia Governor Glenn Stevens has long complained that the currency is fundamentally overvalued and needs to fall to help the domestic economy cope with a cooling mining boom.

On Thursday he went a step further by canvassing the case for the central bank itself selling the local dollar.

"Overall, in this episode so far, the Bank has not been convinced that large-scale intervention clearly passed the test of effectiveness versus cost. But that doesn't mean we will always eschew intervention," Stevens told the Australian Business Economists' annual dinner.

"In fact we remain open-minded on the issue," he added. "Our position has long been, and remains, that foreign exchange intervention can, judiciously used in the right circumstances, be effective and useful."

The local dollar, known in markets as the Aussie, has been holding around $0.9300 this week, having been as high as $0.9758 in October and as low as $0.8848 in August. Even at the low point, the RBA had argued the currency was an uncomfortable burden for trade-exposed sectors of the economy.

Stevens has mused on the prospects for intervention before but always came down against it.

Indeed, in his speech he noted there would be costs to the RBA as any foreign assets bought through intervention would certainly yield much less than Australian debt.

It would also open the central bank to "very large valuation risks", should the local dollar not fall as intended, he said.

GLOBAL FORCES

To be effective, any intervention would have to work with fundamentals and not against them, Stevens said, noting there were powerful global forces at work keeping the currency high.

One such force was the massive increase in Australia's terms of trade - what it gets for its resource exports compared with what it pays for imports - over the past decade.

This shift had been so large and so persistent that it was no longer clear that the Aussie would return to levels that used to be considered "normal" around 70 U.S. cents.

"Notwithstanding that, in my view, the Australian dollar is probably above its longer run equilibrium at present, it is far from clear that we can assume that the mean level we saw in the 1980s to the early 2000s will be the relevant one in the future," said Stevens.

Other forces holding the Aussie up included Australia's top notch triple-A credit rating which has made its debt attractive to foreign central banks and sovereign wealth funds.

A lot of offshore money has also flooded into Australia's booming mining sector in recent years, Stevens added.

A further complicating factor, Stevens cited, was the extraordinary monetary policy stimulus being undertaken in the United States, Japan and the euro zone, which has tended to depress their currencies.

While the RBA has cut its cash rate to a record low of 2.5 percent, that is well above the near-zero rates seen in many major economies.

Many analysts suspect the central bank would prefer not to cut rates again, in part to avoid inflating a bubble in Australian home prices, and instead rely on a drop in the Aussie to support the domestic economy. (Reporting by Wayne Cole; Editing by Chris Gallagher)

title: Australian Dollar Slumps To Two-Month Low
text:
The Australian dollar slumped to a two-month low against the U.S. dollar Thursday after the country's central bank chief once more bemoaned the currency's strength and said he was "open minded" on intervening.

Reserve Bank of Australia Governor Glenn Stevens said intervention remained part of the central bank's "toolkit" although it had refrained from undertaking a "large scale" currency weakening exercise in recent years, because it has not been convinced the effectiveness of such a move would outweigh the costs.

"But that doesn't mean we will always eschew intervention," said Mr. Stevens. "Our position has long been, and remains that foreign exchange intervention can, judiciously used in the right circumstances, be effective and useful," the governor added.

The Aussie, as the currency is commonly known, fell to $0.9241 on EBS, its lowest since Sept. 13, following Mr. Stevens remarks to the Australian Business Economists annual dinner in Sydney.

"The fact that the intervention word crept back into the discussion as things at their disposal" put the Australian currency under pressure, said Daragh Maher, a currencies strategist at HSBC in London.

Still, the prospect of the RBA taking such action is unlikely around current levels, said Alvin Tan, a currencies strategist at Societe Generale.

"If it [Australian dollar] went persistently above $1.0 [against the dollar], then yes it [intervention] becomes more of a possibility," added Mr Tan.

The Australian dollar, which most recently traded at $0.9248 against the buck, has not been above $1 since May.

"We think the Aussie will stay soft enough that they (RBA) don't need to intervene," said HSBC's Mr Maher.

According to the International Monetary Fund, the Australian dollar is overvalued by around 10% despite weakening some 12% since April.

Manufacturers and exporters have blamed the Aussie's strength for hurting their profit and putting the nation at a disadvantage against its trading rivals.

Mr. Stevens also expressed his concern again Thursday about the potential damage a persistently strong currency could have on the Australian economy.

"It is at least conceivable that a large and persistent rise in the exchange rate may have effects on the economy beyond those discernible from the experience of the past thirty years," Mr. Stevens said.

LONDON, Nov 21 (Reuters) - The Australian dollar fell to a two-month low against the U.S. dollar on Thursday after the head of the Reserve Bank of Australia said he was "open-minded" about intervening to drive down the value of the local currency.

It fell to $0.9250 in European trade, its lowest since mid-September after RBA governor Glenn Stevens' comments, down from $0.9285 beforehand.

The Australian dollar was also hurt by U.S. Federal Reserve minutes which suggested policymakers in the world's largest economy may soon start scaling back their monetary stimulus, comments that helped lift the U.S. dollar more broadly.

Traded volumes in the Australian dollar were nearly 50 percent higher than their one-month average on the Thomson Reuters platform.

Analysts said the growth-linked, higher-yielding currency was headed lower in the near term as the RBA was showing more discomfort about its value and its impact on the economy.

Stevens upped the ante on Thursday, saying he was "open-minded" on whether to intervene to try to push the Australian dollar lower.

He has long complained that the currency is fundamentally over-valued and needs to fall to help the domestic economy cope with a cooling mining sector.

Earlier in the day, data from the RBA showed that it had sold more Australian dollars in the currency market in October than it usually does, triggering speculation that it is modestly stepping up intervention.

"This is highly unusual. Unbalanced activity on this scale has not been seen for over four years," said Gareth Berry, currency strategist at UBS, referring to the RBA data.

The RBA manages the forex needs of the Australian government and that usually makes up the vast bulk of its spot transactions in any month.

"This latest evidence now suggests the RBA's patience may be running out and that the central bank may have finally begun to lean against the wind - albeit very gently," Berry said.

title: FOREX -Dollar rises to 4-1/2-month high vs yen; Draghi remarks buoy euro
text:
* ECB's Draghi plays down risk of negative deposit rates

* Dollar/yen hits highest since July following Fed minutes

* Minutes revive prospect of U.S. stimulus tapering soon

* Aussie falls; RBA says open-minded on intervention

By Julie Haviv

NEW YORK, Nov 21 (Reuters) - The dollar rose to its highest against the yen in more than four months on Thursday, still benefiting from Federal Reserve minutes released the day before that suggested U.S. policymakers could start scaling back stimulus earlier than expected.

The euro, meanwhile, recovered earlier losses against the dollar after European Central Bank President Mario Draghi played down the possibility of the bank implementing negative deposit rates. Reports on negative rates had pressured the euro on Wednesday, adding to losses after the Fed minutes.

"However, the shift in the policy outlook may continue to weigh on euro/dollar as we see a growing number of ECB officials show a greater willingness to implement negative deposit rates, and the central bank may have little choice but to take unprecedented steps in the coming months as growth and inflation remains subdued," said David Song, currency analyst at DailyFX in New York.

"In turn, the ECB may use a combination of policy tools to combat the threat for deflation and euro/dollar may take a further hit from the next FOMC meeting amid talks of a December taper," he said.

Minutes from the last Federal Open Market Committee meeting in October showed U.S. policymakers felt there was room to begin scaling back the Fed's $85 billion monthly bond purchase program at one of their next few meetings if warranted by economic conditions.

Many market participants expect the Fed to start reducing its bond purchases in March 2014.

Against the Japanese yen, the dollar rose to 101.15 yen, its highest since July 10. It was last up 1.1 percent at 101.08 yen.

The yen came under strong selling pressure as market players expected Japan's monetary policy to stay ultra-loose for some time.

"With U.S. monetary policy officials moving toward tightening while the (Bank of Japan) is fully committed to an expansionist policy, dollar/yen may be finally ready to resume its rally and if it can clear the resistance at 101.50 it may target the yearly highs over the next several weeks," said Boris Schlossberg, managing director of FX strategy at BK Asset Management in New York.

The dollar showed little reaction to a mixed bag of U.S. data. Jobless claims fell in the latest week, while a Mid-Atlantic business survey from the Philadelphia Fed showed its lowest reading since May.

Speaking in Berlin, Draghi said the possibility of negative deposit rates was discussed at the ECB's last policy meeting and there had been no news since then. He also said the central bank did not see deflation materializing.

The euro was last trading up 0.2 percent at $1.3464, not far from the session high of $1.3478 and above an earlier one-week low of $1.3398.

Draghi's comments were interpreted as differing from an unsourced report on Wednesday which said the ECB may consider making banks pay to deposit cash with it overnight and caused the euro to fall. An ECB spokeswoman declined to comment.

Much has been made about the contrast in the monetary policy stances of the ECB and the Fed, but Jane Foley, senior currency strategist at Rabobank in London, said that "until Fed tapering is upon us, euro/dollar will remain well supported in spite of the dovish threats of the ECB."

The euro rose 1.2 percent against the yen to 135.94 yen, after earlier hitting a four-year peak of 136.04 yen.

Earlier, weak French business activity data was offset by better-than-expected German business activity, although a soft reading for the euro zone as a whole continued to point to a fragile economic recovery.

Sterling hit a four-year high of 163.23 yen and was last changing hands up 1.3 percent at 163.14 yen.

Elsewhere, the Australian dollar fell sharply after Reserve Bank of Australia Governor Glenn Stevens said he was "open-minded" on intervention to push the currency lower.

The Aussie last traded at US$0.9218, down 1.2 percent, according to Reuters data.

title: DJ  Australian Dollar Hits Two-Week Low on Fukushima Incident, Fed Jitters
text:
SYDNEY--The Australian dollar hit a two-week low of US$0.9018, as traders viewed the latest radioactive leak at Fukushima as another reason to sell the embattled currency before the release of Federal Reserve minutes later Wednesday.

The minutes of the Fed's July meeting could back a plan to reduce the central bank's bond buying.

Japan's Nuclear Regulation Authority said the leak of an estimated 300 metric tons (79,000 gallons) of highly contaminated water at the Fukushima Daiichi nuclear power plant represented a level-3 serious incident on the international scale to measure accidents at nuclear facilities.

Late Wednesday, the Aussie was trading at US$0.9035, compared with US$0.9065 late Tuesday.

"News of radioactive water leaking from Fukushima placed downward pressure on the risk-sensitive Australian dollar," CMC Markets senior trader Tim Waterer said. "Even aside from this, the Aussie was looking softer as investors expect upcoming Fed minutes could be supportive of the U.S. dollar if the rhetoric points towards a winding down of stimulus measures."

The Australian dollar was also under pressure because of its strong correlation to the currencies of emerging Asian nations, which have suffered a capital flight caused by the prospect of the Fed's reduced monetary stimulus.

On Wednesday, the Indonesian rupiah hit a fresh four-year low despite Tuesday's intervention by the Indonesian central bank.

The Reserve Bank of Australia's bias toward lower interest rates was another negative factor.

In the minutes of its August board meeting released Tuesday, the RBA said its members agreed that the bank should neither close off the possibility of reducing rates further, nor signal an imminent intention to reduce rates further.

"Heading into what shapes as a very important offshore session, any adverse reaction from commodities and any pro-U.S. dollar sentiment this evening could see the Australian dollar losing hold of the US$0.9000 level," CMC's Mr. Waterer said.

title: 3rd UPDATE: Asian Shares Mixed; HK,  Australia  Up On PBOC Comments
text:
-- Hong Kong, Australia gain, PBOCintervention.

-- Chinese banks recover strongly in Hong Kong.

-- Nikkei pares gains as yen strengthens.

(Adds information, quotes, updates/adds market levels)


 
  By Daniel Inman 
 

Signs that China's credit crunch is starting to ease pushed stocks in Hong Kong and Australia higher, but elsewhere worries lingered over the health of the banking system even after the Chinese central bank moved to reassure investors.

Markets in the region have been increasingly anxious over a liquidity squeeze that some feared could start to threaten growth in Asia's biggest economy. While some of the worries dissipated Wednesday as liquidity conditions eased slightly after the People's Bank of China said Tuesday it would try to bring to an end the squeeze, it wasn't enough to aid Shanghai where the benchmark index fell 0.4%.

Signs of continued stress showed up in the bond market too, where China had to pay higher borrowing costs at a $2.1 billion government bond sale in Hong Kong's offshore yuan market. The Ministry of Finance sold three-year bonds at a coupon of 2.87%, far higher than the 1.85% it paid at its last sale of similar bonds in 2012.

"Local banks have been facing problems of tight yuan liquidity recently, because of the cash crunch in mainland China in recent weeks," said Becky Liu, a Standard Chartered analyst. "Therefore they can't support the auction as much this time round."

Executives also stressed their worries with Mark Cutifani, Chief Executive of giant miner Anglo American, saying the fallout from the cash crunch could mean less investment in China which would hurt commodities. Copper and Nickel have both fallen to their lowest level in years this week, while gold fell as much as 2.6% Wednesday and silver dropped 4%.

But there were reasons for some optimism, with China's seven-day repurchase agreement rate--a benchmark of borrowing costs between banks- falling to 7.30%, down from 7.44% at Tuesday's close. That followed the central's bank statement Tuesday saying it had introduced funds to some financial institutions in recent days, providing relief for cash-strapped banks.

Chinese stocks listed in Hong Kong recovered, with the Hang Seng China Enterprises index jumping 3.3% to 9164.64 - its second gain in the last 20 sessions. The index was helped by banks that have fallen heavily in recent weeks. Industrial and Commercial Bank of China gained 6.8% and China Construction Bank advanced 6.5%.

China Minsheng Banking Corp., one of the banks that was sold off particularly hard, rallied 6.3% in Hong Kong, but its Shanghai-listing was down 1.7%.

Australia, a country with strong trade ties to China also made a gain, with the S&P/ASX 200 up 1.6% to 4731.70 - breaking a four-session losing streak.

title: DJ New Zealand  Currency Intervention  Draws Criticism
text:
WELLINGTON--New Zealand's central bank sold much less of its local currency holdings last month than economists had been expecting, prompting charges it misled markets over the extent of the intervention in order to help drive down the soaring currency.

Earlier this month, the Reserve Bank of New Zealand forewarned that it had "intervened" in currency markets in April to help ease pressure on the country's exporters grappling with an elevated Kiwi, which has risen about 10% in the past year against a basket of currencies. The New Zealand dollar dropped nearly a cent against the U.S. dollar on that announcement.

While the central bank routinely buys and sells small amounts of the currency to support liquidity, the Reserve Bank's explicit reference to intervention was the first since 2007, leading some economists and strategists to believe the April sell-off would be significantly higher than the 256 million New Zealand dollar (US$208 million) figure subsequently announced Thursday. Some economists had expected a figure of as much as NZ$1 billion.

Earlier Thursday, Gov. Graeme Wheeler said the central bank was prepared to step up its intervention in the foreign-exchange market if circumstances demanded it, pushing the Kiwi lower by almost half a cent against the greenback.

Annette Beacher, Singapore-based head of Asia-Pacific research at TD Securities, said the final number for April fell "far short" of expectations.

"Does this confirm that all along that it is merely jawboning the currency lower?" she said. "We question the wisdom of such announcements of intervention by senior RBNZ staff when the evidence clearly shows a lack of resolve."

Alex Sinton, Auckland-based director of institutional foreign exchange at Australia & New Zealand Banking Group, was also critical.

"It was misleading, absolutely, the governor deliberately played it up," he said. "Clearly the amount was insignificant. What will be interesting will be May's numbers."

The central bank said it had no comment on the suggestion its use of the word intervention was misleading.

Central banks in Australia, New Zealand and parts of Asia have been stepping up moves to deal with an influx of international capital as investors scour the globe looking for higher returns in countries where interest rates remain relatively high following the global financial crisis. The inflows have kept currencies such as the Aussie and Kiwi strong, while complicating efforts to manage growth.

Australia's central bank has cut interest rates to a record low 2.75%--still above the U.S. and much of Europe--and at its monthly policy meetings frequently notes the stubborn strength of the Australian dollar. New Zealand's benchmark cash rate is at 2.5%, where it's been since March 2011 to help the economy recover from a series of devastating earthquakes.

Elsewhere, China is moving to curb bets on the rising yuan, while Thailand this month was looking at ways to deal with the strongest baht since the 1997 Asian financial crisis.

The last time New Zealand's central bank officially said it had intervened in the currency market was in 2007, when it was also seeking to bring down the currency. It sold nearly NZ$1.5 billion in June of that year and about NZ$1.6 billion between February and June 2008.

"The timid nature of this intervention suggests that the RBNZ doubts its effectiveness and is prepared to only act to counter spikes higher," said Greg Gibbs, a foreign-exchange strategist at Royal Bank of Scotland, who is based in Singapore. "This activity is much below the more aggressive actions undertaken in 2007-08."
