title: ANALYSIS-Policy patience seen wearing thin as yen drops
text:
* Signs policymakers increasingly concerned over hot money

* Australia, Korea cut rates, NZ intervenes

* Yen drops raises tensions ahead of G7

* Are China measures a template for others?

By Vidya Ranganathan

SINGAPORE, May 10 (Reuters) - The yen's fall past 100 per dollar highlights growing concerns about ultra-loose monetary policy around the globe and raises the prospect that policymakers elsewhere may take action to protect their economies from a tide of hot money.

Fears that a global currency war is brewing were fuelled when the Reserve Bank of Australia and Bank of Korea both cut interest rates this week, citing the strength of their currencies as one of the reasons to act.

New Zealand's central bank, meanwhile, confessed for only the second time since 1985 that it had intervened in currency markets, one of the few defences against the inflows of cheap money for what is an open, but small, economy.

Korea's rate cut on Thursday was a surprise and the central bank Governor Kim Choong-soo made it clear the weakness of the yen was an issue.

Jonathan Cavenagh, a strategist at Westpac Bank in Singapore, said since the Bank of Korea decision the yen had fallen to 101.30 per dollar from 99.00. That had probably not gone unnoticed in South Korea, which competes head on with Japan in many export markets such as auto and technology.

"I can only imagine their concern level has risen a notch or two," he said.

Cavenagh reckoned Bank of Korea's worries were more around how the appreciating won would affect earnings of the country's shipbuilders and electronics exporters, rather than hot money inflows, which have been relatively subdued into that economy.

"But hot money still tends to drive currencies higher and, in an environment where export growth is slowing around the region, it will certainly be creating some headaches," he said.

FRICTION AHEAD OF G7

The yen slid to a 4-year low on Friday and has declined more than 20 percent against the dollar in the past six months as Japan Prime Minister Shinzo Abe pushed his potent mix of aggressive monetary easing and fiscal expansion.

That involved the Bank of Japan (BOJ) unveiling unprecedented monetary expansion on April 4, aiming to revive an economy that has suffered low-grade deflation and sluggish growth for 15 years.

Friday's drop in the Japanese currency was in part driven by the dollar, which was boosted by stronger U.S. data and talk the Federal Reserve, which also has an extraordinarily loose monetary policy, may begin to withdraw some of the stimulus introduced in the aftermath of the global financial.

Ahead of a Group of Seven financial leaders' meeting in Britain, BOJ Governor Haruhiko Kuroda reiterated Japan's position on Friday that its super-loose monetary policy does not target the currency. U.S. Treasury Secretary Jack Lew warned that America was watching.

"Japan has growth issues for a long period of time that we have encouraged Japan to address. So as long as they stay within those bounds of those international agreements I think growth is an important priority," Lew told the CNBC news channel in London.

"I'm just going to refer back to the ground rules and the fact that we've made clear that we'll keep an eye on that," he added.

CAPITAL CONTROLS RESISTED SO FAR

The yen was given a further push down on Friday by Japanese data showing that domestic investors had turned into net buyers of foreign bonds in the past two weeks, backing long-held expectations Abe's policies could drive capital out of the country.

Faced with inflows of capital, policymakers in emerging Asia have so far resisted outright capital controls, such as punitive taxes or investment curbs.

Money has been going into markets in Southeast Asia's high-yielding economies for months, and continues to do so despite the growing risks policymakers may take measures to counter the capital flows. Stock markets in Malaysia and Indonesia have hit record highs and in Singapore a multi-year high.

An appreciating baht has become the subject of a rare and public feud on policy between Thailand's fiercely independent central bank and its finance minister. The Philippines has had to cut a rate on special deposits it uses to manage peso liquidity, in order to moderate the inflows.

The Reserve Bank of New Zealand's governor, Graeme Wheeler, managed to knock around half a cent off the New Zealand dollar

after divulging at a parliamentary committee that it had been active in currency markets, but his success may be limited.

"Until such time as the forces of global QE come to an end it is likely to be the case that the NZ dollar will remain 'overvalued', when measured according to traditional metrics," said Sean Keane of Triple-T Consulting.

"The RBNZ knows that the currency firepower that it has at its disposal would be quickly overwhelmed in any outright assault on the FX market, and large losses may accrue to the bank's balance sheet."

China may, however, have upped the ante in the battle to control hot money flows with measures it carried out last week after the yuan rose to persistent record highs against the dollar.

Regulators tightened limits on long-yuan positions that banks can hold for their own accounts and imposed limits to discourage firms from using dollar loans as a means to speculate on yuan gains.

China's State Administration of Foreign Exchange (SAFE) also said it would increase scrutiny on exporters who channel money into the country disguised as trade payments.

"To me, SAFE's response over the weekend is perhaps a hint of where we are headed," said Westpac's Cavenagh.

"Other central banks around the region may take their lead from China but, of course, they tend to have more open capital account and some of these rules may be difficult to enforce."

title: UPDATE 1-Australia jobless rate rises to 3yr high in March
text:
(Adds market, analyst reaction, detail)

* Employment falls 36,100 in March, after Feb's 74,000 jump

* Jobless rate disappoints with rise to 5.6 pct

* Market narrows odds on another cut in interest rates

By Wayne Cole

SYDNEY, April 11 (Reuters) - Australia's jobless rate rose unexpectedly to hit its highest in over three years in March as employment fell and more people went looking for work, a disappointing report that led markets to narrow the odds on another cut in interest rates.

The Australian dollar eased off recent highs after Thursday's data from the Australian Bureau of Statistics showed the unemployment rate rose to 5.6 percent in March, from 5.4 percent the month before. That was above expectations for a steady outcome and the highest reading since November 2009.

Employment fell by a larger-than-expected 36,100, but that followed a huge forecast-busting 74,000 increase in February. Averaging the two months, employment growth was still reasonably solid.

"We gave back some of those spectacular gains from the last month," said Michael Blythe, chief economist at Commonwealth Bank of Australia.

"At the moment they need about 25,000 jobs a month to stop unemployment from rising, so it's not quite enough. This (data) only reinforces the view the Reserve Bank has an easing bias."

Since cutting rates in October and December, the Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) has been on hold at 3 percent amid signs the stimulus was slowly working though the economy.

Yet it has also left the door open to an easing should it be needed to support demand. The flow of recent data had showed enough of a pick up, particularly in retail sales, for the market to shave expectations on a cut.

But the jobs numbers seemed to put an easing back on the table. Swap rates now imply around 24 basis points of easing ahead, compared to 16 before the data.

Still, a move is considered unlikely at the next policy meeting in May, in part because the very volatility of the jobs figures might lessen their impact on policy.

So big was February's rise that some analysts suspected much of it might be statistical noise which could be reversed in March.

MORE WHOLESALING THAN MANUFACTURING

The ABS releases the industry breakdown of employment quarterly. The latest report for the three months to February, which was out last month, showed wholesaling accounted for the lions share of new jobs, perhaps reflecting the huge growth of online sales and services.

Also adding jobs were healthcare -- the single biggest employer of all -- public administration, education, construction, and hotels and restaurants.

Job losses were concentrated in manufacturing, which has been suffering mightily under the weight of a high currency.

Just this week, General Motors announced 500 jobs losses at its Australian unit, Holden, and blamed the currency for its inability to compete with Japanese and South Korean carmakers.

So far though, policy makers have resisted all calls to try and rein in the currency, in large part because they doubt intervention would work.

RBA Assistant Governor Christopher Kent on Wednesday said there were sign industry was learning to live with a high dollar by becoming more productive and the central bank was a long way from having to consider extreme measures such as intervention.

title: Australia dlr rises to 3mth highs on USD, China trade helps
text:
* Aussie lifted to loftiest since late Jan vs USD

* China imports from Australia jump to 8-mth top

* Aussie trade weighted index surges to 28-yr peak

* Antipodeans hold near multi-year highs vs yen

By Gyles Beckford and Cecile Lefort

SYDNEY/WELLINGTON, April 10 (Reuters) - The Australian and New Zealand dollars rose on Wednesday after strong Chinese imports data pointed to solid demand for the countries' resources, lifting both currencies to multi-decade highs in trade-weighted terms.

Chinese imports from Australia were the highest in eight months in March having climbed 18.4 percent on a year earlier, a boon for export earnings.

The reading sent the Aussie as far as $1.0518, its highest in nearly three months.

"It was supported by stronger imports in China" said Greg Gibbs, a strategist at Royal Bank of Scotland in Singapore, adding high expectations of further quantitative easing in the United States and Japan also helping.

The Aussie was last at $1.0509, from $1.0484 early, with traders quoting heavy option resistance around $1.0520.

A sustained break above $1.0500 should pave the way for a test of the 2013 high around $1.0600. Strong support was seen at $1.0412, the 61.8 percent retracement of its January-March slide.

Despite the Aussie's strength Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) Assistant Governor Christopher Kent said the central bank was a long way from considering intervention.

The next hurdle will be Australia's labour report on Thursday since forecasts are for a dip of 5,000 in March as payback for a startlingly strong increase of 71,500 the month before.

The New Zealand dollar was strong at $0.8530, a whisker away from an 18-month peak of $0.8538 touched overnight.

The kiwi looked destined to push higher in the current positive global risk climate.

"There seems very little to stand in the way of the New Zealand dollar, which has rebounded strongly with capital outflows from defensive currencies back into resource cross pairs," said CMC Markets trader Andrew May.

Near-term resistance was seen at the year high of $0.8538 and then last September's $0.8545 high, while support sits around $0.8490.

The Aussie and kiwi trade-weighted indices shot up to new highs, mostly helped by the Bank of Japan's (BOJ) aggressive monetary easing plan announced last week. The yen is the second biggest component in both indices.

The Aussie index soared to 79.5, its highest since 1985, while the kiwi scaled a fresh lifetime peak of 78.45.

The Aussie also fetched 104.13 yen, having hit a 4-1/2-year high around 104.35 overnight, while the kiwi stood at 84.47, very near 84.75 yen, its strongest in five years.

The Antipodeans have been boosted by expectations some of the new yen printed by the BOJ will find its way into better-yielding assets offshore, either directly or through carry trades.

That in part helped explain why Australian government bonds have been stellar performers of late, particularly at the longer-end of the curve.

Yields of sovereign 10-year debt were last at 3.26 percent, having skidded as low as 3.19 percent earlier this week. Australia is one of the very few countries still enjoying a stable triple A rating while paying some of the highest returns in the developed world.

Australian government bond futures held near multi-month peaks set earlier in the week. The three-year contract was unchanged at 97.220, while the 10-year contract dipped 0.01 point to 96.750, not far from a four-month peak of 96.815 touched Monday.

Data out in New Zealand showed electronic retail card sales fell for the first time in six months in March, amid signs growth in consumer spending was slowing down.

Attention will turn to manufacturing data and speeches by a Reserve Bank of NZ senior official and the Finance Minister on Thursday.

New Zealand government bonds were mostly firmer, with yields as much as 5 basis point lower at the long end of the curve.

title: Australia's Opposition Treasurer Says No 'Correct' Value For A$
text:
SYDNEY--Australia's main opposition party will pursue a hands-off approach to the strong Australian dollar if it wins an election scheduled for September, and use global forums to push back against governments interfering in currency markets.

In a keynote speech, opposition treasurer Joe Hockey steered clear of populist rhetoric on the Australian dollar, and said businesses need to embrace the positives arising from a strong currency.

The comments come as the Aussie dollar continues to trade near record highs against the U.S. dollar.

"There is no 'correct' value for the Australian dollar," Mr. Hockey said. "We can look over time at how it has moved relative to its fundamental drivers but that does not mean that any particular value is right or wrong."

Earnings for manufacturers and exporters have been crimped by the strong Aussie dollar, and the central bank has responded by sharply easing monetary policy to stoke growth in non-mining sectors such as retail and manufacturing.

Opinion polls show the center-right Liberal-National coalition is favored to win the election due Sept. 14, with opposition leader Tony Abbott stretching his lead over Prime Minister Julia Gillard of the Labor Party in recent weeks

Mr. Hockey leaned against suggestions from some academics, lawmakers and trade union groups that the Reserve Bank of Australia should intervene to weaken the exchange rate.

"We would need to be extremely cautious in tinkering with such a successful policy measure," said Mr. Hockey.

The RBA holds primary responsibility for the exchange rate's stability and has repeatedly said that while it has the option of intervention, such a move is unlikely.

Currency levels have become a politically charged issue globally as governments seek to weaken their exchange rates in an effort to boost growth.

Aggressive monetary moves by central banks including the U.S. Federal Reserve and Bank of Japan has contributed to a sharp appreciation in currencies such as the Australian dollar, as foreign investors seek higher-yielding assets.

"We would also take a more pro-active stance in international forums to advocate for less government interference in currency markets," said Mr. Hockey.

"It is in the best interests of all nations that currency values reflect their relative comparative advantage and that trade and capital flows take place at prices set by the market. Australia is a prime example of the benefits that can flow from a 'cleanly' floating currency and we must be a strong advocate of the global advantages of this system," he said.

Since Japanese Prime Minister Shinzo Abe took office in December, a policy of aggressive public comment by his administration has sent the yen sharply lower, drawing the ire of rival exporting nations, though Tokyo escaped any censure in a recent meeting of finance ministers from the Group of 20 largest economies.

title: POLL: Aussie & kiwi dollars to stay doggedly high
text:

SYDNEY, Feb 7 (Reuters) - The Australian and New Zealand dollars are expected to be well supported in the months ahead thanks in part to a lack of high yielding alternatives, even as the Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) could resume easing this year.

A Reuters poll of 52 analysts put the Aussie at $1.0400 until August, before edging slightly lower to $1.020 by this time next year. It last traded at $1.0316.

But the forecasts ranged from a low of 85 cents to a high of $1.1200 for the 12-month view, suggesting the usual uncertainty in the outlook.

The Aussie's strength is one reason why economist expect the Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) to cut its cash rate by 25 basis points to a historical low of 2.75 percent later this year, while swap rates show some risk of a move to 2.5 percent.

After cutting rates in October and December, the central bank held steady at 3 percent this week, citing signs past cuts were slowly working their magic on the economy.

A survey of 48 analysts showed expectations for an equally resilient New Zealand dollar. The median forecast was for the kiwi to be at $0.8400 in one month, before gradually nudging lower to $0.8070 in 12 months.

The kiwi last traded at $0.8359, having jumped to a 1-1/2-year high this week.

The strength of both Antipodean currencies is partly due to signs of stabilisation in China's economy, a key export market, and solid investor appetite for the relatively high yields of Australian and New Zealand government bonds.

Australia and New Zealand 10-year bonds

yield 3.4 percent and 3.7 percent, respectively, compared with less than 2 percent for their equivalent German and U.S. counterparts.

For investors to dump the Aussie or kiwi, they would have to buy some other currency, and attractive alternatives are few and far between.

Central banks in the United States, Japan, UK and Switzerland have been adding to the supply of their currencies either through quantitative easing or outright intervention.

title: DJ Expect the Aussie Dollar to Take off Again
text:
--Glenn Stevens is not too worried about the AUD's rise

--Further RBA interest rate cuts might be limited now

--Mr. Stevens appears unenthusiastic about intervention

--Improving Chinese growth may lift Australia's prospects

By Nicholas Hastings

The Australian dollar's recent rally may be on pause at the moment.

But that doesn't mean that it has stopped.

In fact, reading between the lines of an interview with Reserve Bank of Australia Governor Glenn Stevens this week, there might well be reason to support the Aussie even more than before.

Not only did Mr. Stevens play down suggestions that the Australian currency was overvalued but he implied that the RBA wasn't that keen to bring it down, either through lower interest rates or through market intervention.

On interest rates, Mr. Stevens noted that the Aussie has been benefiting because rates in "global money centers" are at zero, making Australian interest rates, which were cut to 3% from 3.25% earlier this month, still attractive even though they are already at historic lows.

Although the RBA could cut interest rates further, the RBA Governor talked about the "limits to fine tuning".

Analysts at National Australia Bank pointed out that with Mr. Stevens also making it clear that he did not want to preside over another upturn in house price inflation, the RBA is unlikely to keep on cutting the cash rate to 2% or below next year.

So there is little reason to expect that Australian interest rates are going to seriously undermine the attraction of the Australian currency at this stage.

Although there have been rumors in the past that the RBA has attempted to massage the Aussie lower with covert market intervention, Mr. Stevens also made it clear in a rare newspaper interview that this was not an option he is pursuing actively at the moment.

He noted that for intervention to work in driving the Aussie lower, the RBA would have to buy U.S. dollars, which would leave the central bank with a negative carry position, given that U.S. interest rates are essentially down at zero.

On top of that, the RBA would be taking the risk of amassing dollar reserves that could then decline in value.

So, in short, it looks as if the RBA would not stand in the way of further Australian dollar gains at the same time as the currency could find itself becoming more attractive to the international investment community.

After a year of worrying about a global economic recession and the impact this could have on commodity-reliant countries such as Australia, investors are ending 2012 in a much more upbeat mood.

The global recovery may remain uncertain but, with the U.S. now showing more consistent signs of an upturn and China pledging itself to more growth-oriented policies, the export prospects for Australia are probably looking better now than they have for many months.

On Tuesday this week, the World Bank raised its growth forecasts for China and Asia, lifting its 2013 Chinese GDP estimate to 8.4% from a forecast of 8.1% in October.

With that sort of growth upgrade coming through, and with the RBA proving less concerned about the Aussie's rally than many in the market had anticipated, chances are that the Australian currency, which rose from a low under $1.0150 back in October to nearly $1.0600 a week ago, will start to extend its gains again even though it has now slipped back close to $1.0500.

title: IMF plan no signal of bigger reserve role for Aussie dollar -RBA
text:
* IMF plan confirms importance of AUD, CAD globally

 * RBA's Stevens says it's just a classification change

 * RBA plays down talk of 'passive intervention' 

 SYDNEY, Nov 21 (Reuters) - Australia's central bank, grappling with a stubbornly high  currency, said an IMF plan to give the Australian dollar a higher profile in central banks' reserves data did not signal any potentially greater role as a reserve currency.

 The IMF is considering adding the Australian and Canadian dollars next year to a list of separately identified currencies in its database on the currency composition of official foreign exchange reserves (COFER).

 Analysts said the designation could in the long term cement the Australian dollar's position further among reserve currencies, while near-term implications were seen limited since many central banks in the Asia-Pacific region already hold the currency.

 But any resultant increased demand that would further lift  the currency's value would be a worry for the central bank, as it would hurt exports in the non-resource sectors just as a mining investment boom looks set to peak in 2013 or 2014.

 Currently, participating central banks report their holdings of both commodity-oriented currencies under the "other" category, while the U.S. dollar, euro, yen, sterling and Swiss franc are individually listed.

Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) Governor Glenn Stevens said there was not much significance in the plan, calling it a "classification change" and nothing more.

 "That actually isn't any sort of particular endorsement that makes us more of a reserve currency than we were," he told a dinner late on Tuesday in Melbourne.

 "We've in fact been a small reserve currency for quite a few countries for probably 25 years," he said, adding that most Asian central banks have held substantial holdings of the local dollar for a while.

 Stevens said no one knows exactly how much in Australian dollars the region's central banks hold, but the IMF reclassification could shed light on that. 

 AUSSIE IN DEMAND

 The Australian dollar, or Aussie, has been highly sought after following the global financial crisis, given the country's top-notch credit ratings and relatively higher interest rates. 

 The resource-rich economy is also the envy of the developed world, having escaped the worst of the global financial turmoil and boasting annual growth of 3 percent or more. 

 Solid foreign demand helped to explain why the Aussie has held up so well over the past two years despite a savage drop in the prices of some of the country's top exports such as iron ore.

 The IMF plan confirms the importance of both the Australian and Canadian dollars to reserve managers and asset allocators globally, said Sean Keane at Triple T Consulting.

 "The IMF's acknowledgement of this may encourage those who have not yet diversified their reserves more widely to consider doing so," said Keane, who works on behalf of Credit Suisse.

 "No matter how insignificant the direct impact of this change is, it will be read by investors as a signal of strength in both currencies, and in those two economies."

 The move by the IMF is part of a wider review to provide more transparency in global financial data. It is also a reflection of a growing trend by central banks around the world to diversify their holdings beyond the U.S. dollar, the euro and the yen.

 But global investors have already been scrambling to buy the Aussie dollar, noted Gavin Stacey, strategist at Barclays Capital, said. "(This) may not give the currency much more upside than would otherwise be the case," he said.

 The Australian dollar has been largely trading within a $1.0150 to $1.0450 range over the past few months. Last year, it peaked around $1.1080, the highest since it was floated in late 1983.

 On a trade-weighted basis, the Aussie dollar is at 77.1

against a basket of currencies, not far from its historic high near 79.0.

 RBA data revealed it has been accumulating foreign currencies in the last three months at a much faster pace than at any time during the past three years, raising suspicion that it was trying to ease upward pressure on the Aussie via direct sales to foreign central banks that wanted to increase reserves of the currency. 

 But Stevens on Tuesday dismissed suggestions the bank intended any "stealth intervention" in the currency markets, saying: "That was customer business that we decided to keep on the balance sheet because the prices seem attractive to do that at this time." 

(Reporting by Ian Chua; Editing by Edmund Klamann)

title: UPDATE:  Australia 's RBA Persists With Passive  Intervention
text:
--Foreign exchange reserves grow further in October

--RBA adopts stealthy intervention to lower A$

--Foreign central banks might be behind reserves' rise

(Adds reaction by economists from the third paragraph.)

By James Glynn

SYDNEY--Australia's central bank continued to apply subtle downward pressure on the Australian dollar in October by allowing its foreign currency reserves to grow.

The Reserve Bank of Australia, or RBA, allowed its foreign currency holdings to rise by 457 million Australian dollars (US$473 million) during the month, adding to a rise of A$891 million in the previous two months, compared with an average of just under A$50 million in the second quarter. Normally the central bank would balance the inflow by buying Australian dollars in the spot market.

"This is yet more evidence that the RBA is using its reserves management in some form of passive intervention," said Paul Bloxham, chief economist at HSBC, Australia.

The strong Australian dollar, trading up 7.5% since hitting its year-low in June, remains a drag on certain areas of the economy such as tourism and manufacturing. The currency is also blamed by energy and mining companies for adding to development costs and undermining the competitiveness of Australia's crucial resource exports. Despite 1.5 percentage points of interest rate cuts over the last year and a fall in the price of key industrial commodity exports such as coal and iron ore, the Aussie dollar has refused to respond by moving lower.

By allowing its foreign currency reserves to grow, the RBA is using one of the only tools it has left, short of full intervention, to manage the currency. The RBA last openly intervened to influence the level of the currency during the global financial crisis in 2008, when it vigorously defended the Australian dollar as it plunged 40% in the space of weeks.

Australia is suffering as countries such as the U.S. and Japan persist with policies to devalue their currencies, Mr. Bloxham said.

The central bank isn't alone amongst smaller nations now using foreign currency reserves as a policy tool. Denmark's central bank in September reversed a policy of selling the Danish kroner on-and-off for the past 18 months in an effort to slow the krone's appreciation against the European common currency.

At the same time, foreign currency inflows from central banks continue to be blamed for helping to keep the Aussie dollar at elevated levels. Central banks from Berlin to Beijing have been linked to buying Australian dollar assets and Australian regional and government bonds continue to attract strong demand from overseas given their relative low risk and high yield. Around 80% of Australia's AAA-rated government bonds on issue are owned by foreign entities, compared with 35% in 2002, official figures show.

At 0110 GMT, the Australian dollar was trading at US$1.0357, down from an earlier intraday high of US$1.0375. title: DJ  Australia 's RBA Continues Passive A$  Intervention  In October
text:
SYDNEY--Australia's central bank continued to apply subtle downward pressure on the Australian dollar in October by allowing its foreign currency reserves to grow.

The Reserve Bank of Australia, or RBA, allowed its foreign currency reserves to rise by 457 million Australian dollars (US$473 million) during the month, adding to a rise of A$420 million in September and A$471 million in August.

The RBA seldom intervenes overtly in the currency market and it hasn't disclosed any official change in its reserves policy. But normally it would balance the inflows by buying Australian dollars in the spot market.

Foreign currency inflows from central banks have been a key factor in keeping the Australian dollar elevated in 2012. Despite large falls in commodity prices and significant interest rate cuts, the Australian dollar has traded above parity with the greenback for nearly all of 2012.

The strong currency is hurting exporters as well as retailers and tourism operators, making their goods relatively more expensive and encouraging Australians to travel and shop overseas.

RBA Governor Glenn Stevens said last week the Australian dollar "remains higher than might have been expected, given the observed decline in export prices and the weaker global outlook."

title: Australia  cenbank sets very high bar for A$  intervention
text:
SYDNEY, Oct 30 (Reuters) - A top Australian central banker on Tuesday said intervening on a large scale to bring down the high local dollar would be a very big step which would only be taken "in extremis".

Asked about the chance of selling the Australian dollar to bring it lower, Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) Deputy Governor Philip Lowe said a floating currency had been of huge benefit to the country and tampering with that by intervening could have adverse consequences.

Answering questions after giving a speech on the economy, Lowe said he was a bit surprised the Australian dollar had not eased in recent months given there had been sharp falls in the price of some of the country's key commodity exports.

Yet he also said it was hard to argue that the currency was fundamentally overvalued or that it was harming the local economy in a serious way.

The strength of the Australian dollar has crimped some sectors such as manufacturing and tourism and prompted calls for the central bank to act to bring it down.

Lowe said the fall in prices for some of Australia's commodity exports had led to some pullback in mining investment plans. As a result he now expected the boom in mining investment to peak around the middle of next year, instead of near the end of the year.

title: Australia Central Bank  'Passively'  Intervenes
text:
SYDNEY--Australia's central bank is letting its foreign-currency holdings grow, putting downward pressure on the strong Aussie dollar.

The Reserve Bank of Australia, which very seldom intervenes overtly in the currency market, hasn't disclosed any change in its reserves policy, but normally it would balance the inflow by buying Australian dollars in the spot market. Over the past two months, though, RBA data show reserves have grown by 863 million Australian dollars (US$890 million), compared with a monthly average of A$49 million in the second quarter.

Letting foreign currencies pile up removes what would otherwise be a source of upward pressure on the Aussie dollar. Paul Bloxham, chief economist at HSBC Australia and former senior official at the RBA, called it "passive" intervention by the central bank, which he said doesn't want to manage the currency but is happy to increase the headwinds against it.

"I think the RBA wants a lower currency," he said.

Indeed, the bank has clearly expressed its discomfort with the Aussie's strength, which saps the profitability of the nation's miners and other exporters.

RBA Gov. Glenn Stevens cited the strong currency as a key reason for this month's rate cut, and board member Jillian Broadbent told The Wall Street Journal this week she hopes "the Australian dollar gets a bit weaker going forward as the mining boom eases off." The Aussie has remained above parity with the U.S. dollar since late June, despite the bust in that once-in-a-century mining boom, a steep drop in commodity prices and 1.5 percentage points of RBA interest-rate cuts since November.

The central bank has boosted reserves by not offsetting the "other outright transactions" on its books, as it would normally do to maintain a steady level of reserves. Other outright transactions include the RBA's dealings with other central banks and international financial institutions.

The RBA last openly intervened to influence the level of the currency during the global financial crisis in 2008, when it vigorously defended the Australian dollar as it plunged 40% in the space of weeks.

The Australian dollar was trading at US$1.0337, up from June's 2012 low of less than 96 U.S. cents but off last month's high above US$1.06.

SYDNEY, Oct 4 (Reuters) - The Australian dollar is unlikely to fall much in the months ahead, mainly because of a lack of high yielding alternatives, according to a Reuters poll of analysts, even after the central bank cut interest rates this week.

The median forecast of 50 analysts showed the Aussie

at $1.0390 in a month's time, then $1.0200 in three months, $1.0240 in six months and $1.0100 by this time next year. This compared with $1.0210 where it currently stands.

But the forecasts ranged from a low of $0.8400 to a high of $1.0900 for the 12-month view, suggesting great uncertainty in the outlook.

The resilience of the currency would not sit well with the Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA), which recently said the local dollar remained higher than expected in the face of falling prices of the country's key commodity exports and a weaker growth outlook.

The RBA cut its cash rate by 25 basis points to a three-year low of 3.25 percent on Tuesday and left the door open for more.

A separate survey showed analysts expect an equally resilient New Zealand dollar. The median forecast was for the kiwi to be at $0.8230 in a month, then $0.8150 in three months, $0.8100 in six months and $0.8000 in 12 months. The kiwi currently stands at $0.8200.

yield 3.0 percent and 3.5 percent respectively, compared with roughly 1.5 percent for their equivalent German and U.S. counterparts.

Also for investors to dump the Aussie or kiwi, they would have to buy some other currency, and attractive alternatives are few and far between.

title: High Australian Dollar Challenges Companies - Finance Minister
text:
-High Australian dollar challenges companies - Finance Minister

-Era of rising commodity prices "not continuing" - Finance Minister

-Australia central bank has room to move, if chooses to - Finance Minister

By Alexander Kolyandr

MOSCOW--Australia's economy faces two big challenges, with a pullback in prices for its key commodities exports and a painfully strong currency, but it will still attract new investment, and let the market decide how to value the Australian dollar, its finance minister said Thursday.

Speaking in Moscow to Dow Jones Newswires on the sidelines of the meeting of finance ministers from the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum, Penny Wong said "the era of rising commodity prices is demonstrably not continuing," but "there is still a lot of investment to come [to Australia] in terms of the mining boom."

Ms. Wong said the slowdown in commodity prices poses no risk to the country's finances. The government has never "assumed in the terms of our economic policy and budget settings that [the commodity prices rise] would continue at [earlier] levels," adding that the budget assumes "stepping down in terms of trade and lowering of prices."

She added that as inflation is constrained at the lower end of the target range, the Reserve Bank of Australia "still has room to move in terms of monetary policy, if it chooses to do so." The central bank held interest rates at 3.5% at its most recent meeting earlier this month, but many analysts believe it may need to lower its key rate, particularly if China's economic growth falters notably.

Although the demand for commodities is dropping, Ms. Wong said the country still expects about half a trillion Australian dollars (US$522 billion) of investment in its mining industry, though she didn't specify over what time period.

Ms. Wong's comments add to the persistent drumbeat of warnings that the Australian economy could hit a relatively rough patch. Resources Minister Martin Ferguson said on Aug. 22 that the country's resources boom was over, and last week, Melbourne-based BHP Billiton (BHP.AU), the world's largest mining company by market value, cut or deferred billions of dollars in proposed investments, shelving a US$30 billion Olympic Dam project.

Deutsche Bank said last week there is "dangerous complacency" about the risk for the Australian economy given the slide in commodity prices over recent months. It said the pace of decline is consistent with a potential recession in 2013.

One knock-on effect of the boom in Australia's commodities exports in recent years, and of persistent demand for its triple-A rated government bonds, has been a push higher in its currency. Ms. Wong noted that the Australian dollar had been "very high in recent times," attributing that to the "the strength of the economy."

The currency has struggled over the past three weeks, falling Thursday to under US$1.03 against the U.S. dollar from above US$1.06 on Aug. 9, with strategists attributing the latest weakness to the continued plunge in key iron ore spot prices to a three-year low and pessimistic comments from the Chinese steel sector.

Still, the Australian currency is strong by historical standards. It has never traded above US$1.1080, and it has risen by around 70% since the lows struck in the depths of the global financial crisis in 2008. It has traded above parity with the U.S. dollar for most of this year.

Ms. Wong said the high exchange rate has created some real challenges and difficulties to some sectors of the economy and to many firms, notably in manufacturing.

However, she said moving to "floating exchange rate [in 1983] was an important step to Australia, and we remain committed to that."

Any "softening of the currency is the matter of the markets," she said.

On Aug. 24, Australia's top central bank official ruled out Swiss-style intervention to curtail the local currency.

title: RBA Rules Out A$  Intervention
text:
-- Australia's central bank rules out A$ intervention

-- RBA Governor says intervention too risky to taxpayers

-- Governor Stevens says safe-haven buying buoying local unit

SYDNEY--Australia's top central bank official has ruled out Swiss-style intervention to curtail the local currency which is trading near 30-year highs as the world's central banks seek a safe haven in the country's AAA-rated bonds.

Buying massive amounts of foreign currency--as policymakers in Switzerland have done--to put a lid on the currency would be too risky to taxpayers, Glenn Stevens, governor of the Reserve Bank of Australia told lawmakers Friday.

"In extremis, you can argue it should be done but it's a big call and it's not a call we feel should be made at this point in time," he said.

Mr. Stevens' comments, in a twice-yearly appearance before lawmakers in Canberra, strongly signal the central bank is resigned to allowing the market to dictate the Australian dollar's strength.

The Australian dollar has risen by around 70% since lows struck after the global financial crisis in 2008, and has traded consistently above parity with the U.S. dollar so far this year.

Record foreign buying of Australia's government securities has played a part in helping to support the Australian dollar even as commodity prices and global growth slow.

Mr. Stevens highlighted those safe-haven investment flows, hinting that they could prevent the Australian dollar from depreciating as rapidly as it usually would as a resources boom that helped Australia record the fastest growth rate of any developed nation in the first quarter loses steam.

"I think there is a bit of a safe-haven mechanism at work at least some of the time," Mr. Stevens said.

Mr. Stevens said some of the world's biggest central banks, including the Swiss National Bank, are now active buyers of the Australian dollar, allocating significant amounts of their foreign currency reserves into the country.

"I never thought I would ever see such an anti-inflationary conservative institution as (the Swiss National Bank) hold our currency as part of their reserves, it's a remarkable thing," said Mr. Stevens.

Calls have emerged from business and unions for the RBA to act to lower the currency, either through direct intervention or cuts in interest rates. The RBA has stepped up its jaw-boning of the currency in recent weeks, noting its strength despite sharp falls in commodity prices.

A report by the Treasury Department earlier this month said intervention to weaken the Australian dollar would probably fail, and would risk introducing instability into the economy.

The governor said Friday he is "a little surprised" the local unit hasn't fallen more as Australia's terms of trade, or the difference between what the country is paid for exports and what it pays for imports, have weakened and as the global growth outlook has softened.

Prices for iron ore--Australia's biggest export--are now at a 2-1/2-year low, and aluminum and nickel prices are also holding near multi-year lows.

The governor said the Australian dollar wasn't excessively over-valued at current levels. "It is a bit on the high side I would say, but probably not dramatically so," Mr. Stevens said. He declined to say exactly how much weaker the unit should be but said: "we're not talking 20 cents worth". At 0300 GMT, the Australian dollar was at US$1.0436.

The currency has remained robust despite increasing signs that Australia's mining investment boom is slowing, with major miners announcing this week the shelving of multi-billion dollar projects. BHP Billiton Ltd. (BHP) on Wednesday said it would postpone or scale back projects valued at more than US$50 billion, sending the clearest signal yet that the global mining boom has run its course.

In a wide-ranging testimony, Mr. Stevens was also called to account for his action in relation to a bribery scandal enveloping the central bank and two of its banknote making units. The matter involves allegations that the two firms paid agents in Malaysia, Vietnam and elsewhere to help win government banknote-printing contracts.

Mr. Stevens stridently rejected assertions that details of the scandal had been held back from scrutiny. "There was no cover up," he said.

Local media this week reported that senior officials had been aware of malpractices at Securency International Pty. Ltd. and Note Printing Australia as much as two years before police were called in.

--Rachel Pannett in Sydney contributed to this article

title: DJ UPDATE: Australian Treasury Says A$  Intervention  Wouldn't Work
text:
--Australian dollar intervention would fail, says treasury

--Says calls for intervention are misplaced

(Updates with commentary by RBA Assistant Governor in tenth paragraph) 


 
   By James Glynn 
 

SYDNEY--Australia's Treasury Department said Friday that intervention in currency markets to depreciate the near-record Australian dollar would be ineffective or else cause greater macroeconomic instability.

Some business groups and unions have called for policy action to lower the currency--either through direct intervention in currency markets or by lowering interest rates--as exporters unconnected with the country's mining investment boom feel the pain of waning competitiveness.

The Australian dollar has risen about 70% since the global financial crisis in 2008, and currently trades near US$1.0515. The treasury said its rise has been fanned by rising commodity prices, higher relative interest rates and the low-risk environment offered by the country's debt market.

It has risen by around 10% since early June, helped in part by strong international central bank demand for the country's AAA-rated government bonds.

The treasury warned that market intervention was likely to fail and that cutting interest rates would be the best way forward if the strong Australian dollar started to severely harm the broader economy.

"Calls for Australia to shift away from its long-standing policy approach and take action directed at lowering the value of the Australian dollar are misplaced," the treasury said in its latest Economic Roundup. "Rather than helping the economy, the available options are likely to be either ineffective or result in greater macroeconomic instability."

The Australian dollar was weaker after the comments by Treasury. At 0530 GMT, it was trading at US$1.0473, down from an intraday high of US$1.0528.

The Reserve Bank of Australia has plenty of room to cut interest rates from 3.5% if clear signs emerged that the strong currency was harming the economy. It has already cut interest rates by 125 basis points since November.

"If the high exchange rate is judged to be inconsistent with keeping the economy close to non-inflationary full employment, we could expect that monetary policy would be eased in response, putting downward pressure on the Australian dollar," the treasury said.

Its rejection of currency intervention comes after Reserve Bank of Australia Assistant Governor Guy Debelle on Thursday said the central bank had been highlighting for some time the widening gap between the Australian dollar's level and, for example, commodity prices.

By convention, the central bank conducts intervention in the currency market. Since the Australian dollar was floated in 1983, the RBA has intervened on a number of occasions. The last time was after the collapse of Lehman Brothers in September 2008, when it bought Australian dollars.

The central bank highlighted twice last week the growing gap between the level of the Australian dollar and falling commodity prices. Prices for the key exports of iron ore and coal have fallen to two-year lows in recent months.

title: Australia cenbank seen unlikely to act on strong AUD
text:
* Aussie dlr holds painfully firm despite global headwinds

* Calls grow for RBA to intervene to lower currency

* Economy doing well, scope to cut rates first if needed

By Ian Chua

SYDNEY, Aug 17 (Reuters) - Australia's central bank recently warned a persistently high dollar could eventually drag on growth, yet actual intervention seems unlikely with the economy still the envy of the developed world.

Even in the face of slowing growth in China, Australia's single largest export market, the local currency has held up remarkably well. That has spurred calls for the Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) to act to temper its strength.

Car makers such as Ford Motor and General Motor's

Holden unit have cut hundreds of jobs this year as they battle a high currency, even after securing million of dollars of funding from state and federal governments.

Though it has acknowledged the need to subsidise struggling exporters, the federal Treasury on Friday reiterated its view on the Australian dollar, describing calls for its value to be officialy curbed "misplaced".

It said in a research paper: "Rather than helping the economy, the available options are likely to be either ineffective or result in greater macroeconomic instability.

"The combination of flexible inflation-targeting monetary policy and a floating exchange rate has served Australia well in delivering macroeconomic stability through a range of shocks over the past two decades. There is no coherent reason to believe that it is inappropriate for current economic circumstances."

The RBA views the rise of the currency as part of inevitable structural change in an economy driven by a mining boom, to which the affected sectors will just have to adapt.

Last month, RBA Deputy Governor Philip Lowe said it was "hard to make a case that the currency is over-valued".

Part of the reason for the Aussie's strength is the country's stable triple-A credit rating and relatively high central bank cash rate at 3.5 percent, versus near zero in the United States.

That combination has proved too hard to resist for many foreign investors, who now hold around 80 percent of outstanding Australian government bonds, double from 10 years ago.

The Aussie reached a historic peak of $1.1081 last year and has since stayed above parity for much of the time. On a trade weighted basis, it remains near a record high.

Intervention will usually require the RBA to create more Australian dollars to lower the currency's value, and while it can then choose to drain the excess cash from the banking system -- known as sterilisation -- many analysts say doing so will diminish the impact.

But leaving the cash sloshing around the banking system could be inflationary. That would be a risk when the economy is growing near its speed limit and domestically-generated price pressures are running at above 3 percent a year.

"The RBA's view is that the best contribution the monetary authorities can make is to keep inflation low," said Richard Grace, a strategist at Commonwealth Bank.

VAST AMOUNTS, SMALL RESULT

Furthermore, for the Aussie to fall, some other currency will have to strengthen. At a time when major central banks like the Federal Reserve are adding stimulus to their economies, the RBA will have a very big fight on its hand.

Last October, Japan sold a jaw-dropping 8 trillion yen ($101 billion) to weaken its currency. But all that firepower only lifted the dollar about 4 yen to 79.50, which is almost exactly where it is 11 months later.

The RBA is a sceptic of intervention as well. Governor Glenn Stevens earlier this year said he was not attracted to that option, declaring: "I'm not sure it would be effective."

In a research paper released in December, the RBA concluded the effects of intervention are usually short-lived under normal market conditions. It also said determining fair value for any currency is fraught with difficulties.

To be sure, the RBA frequently intervened following the float of the currency in the 1980s, but has since taken a hands-off approach as the market matured. Recently, it has only done so in times of severe market dysfunction.

For the RBA to take that route again, it has to see the benefits outweigh the risks. Given that it recently upped its 2012 growth forecast to a brisk 3.5 percent, analysts said any action is a long way off.

"Intervention is unlikely," said Michael Turner, strategist at RBC, adding the high currency and global headwinds mean the RBA could cut interest rates first.

(Editing by Eric Meijer)

(Recasts first paragraph to include Treasurer's remarks, adds further comment from Swan from second paragraph)

SYDNEY--Australian Treasurer Wayne Swan Thursday welcomed a surprise drop in the unemployment rate in July and predicted that the commodity-rich economy would be the fastest-growing in the developed world through 2013.

"Australia's economic fundamentals remain strong, with our economy expected to grow faster than every major advanced economy this year and next," he said, without citing any specific forecast.

Mr. Swan said Australia was "in a league of its own" after official figures Thursday showed unemployment dropped to 5.2% in July from 5.3% in June as the economy added a modest 14,000 jobs. The upbeat report comes amid calls this week from businesses and unions for the Reserve Bank of Australia to intervene in currency markets to lower the soaring Australian dollar.

The currency is within striking distance of its 30-year highs having risen around 10% since early June, prompting calls for the RBA to help ease the pain for manufacturers whose exports have become less competitive and retailers whose customers are buying more from websites based overseas.

The Aussie dollar touched an intraday high of US$1.0617 in Asia trading Wednesday, compared with US$1.054 late Wednesday.

The high currency is also beginning to hurt mining companies. Resource giants Rio Tinto PLC and BHP Billiton Ltd. have recently cited the strength of the Aussie as adding to their costs while threatening their investments.

Economists said the figures confirming an increase in hiring gave the central bank stronger grounds for keeping rates on hold as opposed to cutting, which might have helped put a brake on the currency's rise. While the RBA is likely to take on board the better jobs figures, it will also be cautious given the continuing vulnerability in Europe's economy.

"It could be that the RBA easing cycle is over," said Citi economist Josh Williamson, whose bank has a November rate cut pencilled in that may now be under review.

"It certainly doesn't validate expectations for an aggressive rate-cut scenario," Mr. Williamson said.

The RBA acknowledged Tuesday that the high currency was an issue for policy makers especially against a backdrop of falling commodity prices, and yet chose to keep interest rates steady at 3.5%.

Following are the top Asia-Pacific stories featured on Dow Jones Newswires as of 0700 GMT. Not all stories appear on all wires. Please direct any questions or comments to asianewseds@dowjones.com.

MACRO/FOREX/FIXED INCOME:


 
UPDATE: RBA KEEPS RATES ON HOLD, SAYS CHINA UNLIKELY TO SLOW FURTHER 

Australia's central bank kept interest rates steady at 3.5% on Tuesday as expected, saying it sees signs that China's economic slowdown has bottomed out, while the local economy continues to grow solidly. (published 0545 GMT)


 
UPDATE: PBOC INJECTS CNY50 BLN INTO MARKET; RAISES EXPECTATIONS FOR EASING 

China's central bank injected 50 billion yuan into the money market via its regular open-market operation Tuesday, making more cash available in the banking system as the world's second-largest economy continues to combat slower-than-expected growth. (published 0508 GMT)


 
NO NEED FOR RBA TO INTERVENE AGAINST STRONG A$ - ECONOMISTS 

Australia's central bank is unlikely to be in a mood to become the Swiss National Bank of the South Pacific and start intervening to prevent further gains in its robust currency, according to economists. (published 0149 GMT)


 
AUSTRALIA'S CENTRAL BANK SHOULD CAP A$ RISE -MORGAN STANLEY

Australia's central bank should cap the nation's rising currency to rescue sectors of the economy that aren't benefiting from a mining boom, Morgan Stanley analysts said. (published 0407 GMT)


 
FITCH: ASIA-PACIFIC BANKS' LEVERAGE, CHINA EXPOSURE POSE RISKS 

Asia-Pacific banks' rising leverage and growing exposure to China will serve as a restraint on their ratings, and could trigger downgrades if conditions in the world's second-largest economy worsen, Fitch Ratings said Tuesday. (published 0309 GMT)


 
UPDATE: JAPAN TAX BILL VOTE TO GO AHEAD BUT PM STILL FACES THREATS OF CENSURE AND NO-CONFIDENCE VOTES 

Japan's main opposition party said Tuesday that it would allow a vote to go ahead on a hotly debated tax increase bill, but it still held out the option of slamming the prime minister with censure or no-confidence measures in a bid to force snap elections. (published 0518 GMT)


 
JAPAN GOVT FUJIMURA: HOPE SALES-TAX BILL PASSES IN ACCORDANCE WITH 3-PARTY AGREEMENT 

Japan's top government spokesman said Tuesday that he hopes that the sales tax bill will pass the upper house of parliament in accordance with the agreement reached between the governing Democratic Party of Japan and the opposition Liberal Democratic and New Komeito parties. (published 0119 GMT)


 
UPDATE: JAPAN EXTENDS SPECIAL MEASURE AS YEN STAYS STRONG 

Japan's finance ministry announced Tuesday a six-month extension to a measure encouraging Japanese firms to buy foreign assets, figuring that further flows of private-sector money out of the country are needed to help tackle the strong yen. (published 0354 GMT)


 
AUSTRALIAN CONSTRUCTION DOWNTURN DEEPENS IN JULY 

A two-year downturn in Australia's construction industry deepened in July adding to evidence that cuts in interest rates since November have done little to support demand. (published 2330 GMT)


 
THAI GOVERNMENT TO RAISE VALUE ADDED TAX RATE TO 9% FROM OCTOBER 2014 VS 7% NOW 

Thailand's cabinet has agreed to raise the value added tax rate to 9% from Oct. 1, 2014, government spokeswoman Sansanee Nakpong said Tuesday. (published 0621 GMT)


 
MALAYSIA SELLS MYR3.50 BLN FEB 2016 GOVT INVESTMENT ISSUES AT AVERAGE YIELD OF 3.235% 

Malaysia sold 3.50 billion ringgit worth of Government Investment Issues maturing February 2016 at an average yield of 3.235%, the central bank said on its website Tuesday. (published 0606 GMT)


 
2ND UPDATE: MONSOON RAINS FLOOD PHILIPPINE CAPITAL, 9 PROVINCES 

The Philippine government ordered some offices and schools closed Tuesday while local financial markets suspended trading, as heavy monsoon rains that started late Monday submerged several areas of the capital Manila and nine other provinces on the main island of Luzon. (published 0519 GMT)


 
UPDATE: NEW ZEALAND 2Q WAGE DATA SUGGESTS UPSIDE TO JOBS RATE FORECAST 

New Zealand wage growth continued to track higher while filled jobs and paid hours rebounded in the second quarter, with economists now forecasting the possibility of better-than-expected employment in the second quarter. (published 0252 GMT)


 
ICBC'S UP TO CNY1 BLN DIM SUM BONDS GET MORE THAN CNY2 BLN OF ORDERS- SOURCE 

Industrial & Commercial Bank of China Ltd.'s three-year offshore yuan-denominated bonds have received more than 2 billion yuan of orders, exceeding its plan to raise up to CNY1 billion through the debt issue, a person familiar with the matter said Tuesday. (published 0638 GMT)

EQUITIES:


 
UPDATE: STANDARD CHARTERED SHARES DIVE 7% ON US REGULATOR'S IRAN ALLEGATIONS 

Standard Chartered PLC's shares in Hong Kong tumbled to their lowest level in more than two and a half years on Tuesday, hit by broker downgrades following allegations by New York's financial regulator that the bank's U.S. unit ran a "rogue institution" that "schemed" with Iran's government to hide illegal transactions. (published 0621 GMT)


 
UPDATE: ESPRIT SURGES AS CEO APPOINTMENT REMOVES OVERHANG 

Esprit Holdings Ltd.'s shares jumped more than 30% Tuesday afternoon as investors welcomed the fashion retailer's announcement that it tapped a senior executive from Zara parent Inditex SA as its new chief executive, resolving a major source of uncertainty that had been weighing on the blue-chip company. (published 0634 GMT)

SINOPEC, ENN EXTEND DEADLINE FOR TALKS ON JOINT BID FOR CHINA GAS TO SEPT 6 

China Petroleum & Chemical Corp., or Sinopec, and gas supplier ENN Energy Holdings Ltd. said Monday they have extended the deadline for the completion of negotiations on their US$2.15 billion planned acquisition of China Gas Holdings Ltd. . (published 0034 GMT)


 
UPDATE: TOKYO BOURSE HALTS DERIVATIVES TRADING DUE TO SYSTEM TROUBLE 

The Tokyo Stock Exchange on Tuesday temporarily suspended all derivatives trading soon after the morning open due to unidentified system problem, the second significant trading glitch on the bourse this year. (published 0207 GMT)


 
UPDATE: BRIDGESTONE 2Q NET PROFIT UP ON EMERGING MARKET DEMAND 

Bridgestone Corp. said Tuesday that its net profit rose 45% on year in the second quarter, as steady demand in emerging markets and robust demand for high-margin tires used in construction and mining vehicles offset faltering sales in Europe and the yen's strength. (published 0649 GMT)


 
UPDATE: KEPPEL SECURES US$4.1 BLN RIG ORDER FROM BRAZIL 

Keppel Corp. has secured its biggest ever single order after signing contracts to build five semisubmersible drilling rigs for Sete Brasil Participacoes SA for US$4.1 billion. (published 0453 GMT)


 
UPDATE: LEIGHTON SWINGS TO 1H PROFIT; ANALYSTS CAUTIOUS ON REVENUE OUTLOOK 

Construction firm and mining contractor Leighton Holdings Ltd. said Tuesday it returned to profitability in the first half, as it completed one troublesome major project and neared the end of another. (published 0352 GMT)


 
WHITEHAVEN COAL TO RESTRUCTURE MANAGEMENT TEAM 

Whitehaven Coal Ltd. is restructuring its management team to handle future growth, the company said Tuesday. (published 0004 GMT)


 
UPDATE: TRANSURBAN MULLS US ROAD DISPOSAL AFTER PROFIT SLIDES 

Transurban Group said Tuesday it's mulling the disposal of a U.S. toll road that drove a 51% slide in its annual profit and indicated its robust Australian assets aren't invincible to softer economic conditions at home. (published 0307 GMT)


 
2ND UPDATE: COCHLEAR PROFIT DENTED BY RECALL, SHARES SINK 

Cochlear Ltd. said net profit plunged 68% in fiscal 2012 after the bionic-ear maker was hit by expenses linked to the voluntary recall of its CI500-series implant. (published 0439 GMT)


 
WSJ: DREAMWORKS PLANS STUDIO IN SHANGHAI 

DreamWorks Animation SKG Inc. on Tuesday signed plans with Chinese partners to build a $350 million movie studio in Shanghai to capitalize on the success of its Kung Fu Panda film franchise as the studio looks to build up its presence in a fast-growing Chinese movie market. (published 0516 GMT)


 
UPDATE: GLOBE 2Q NET DOWN 9.7%; RISING COSTS OUTPACE GROWTH IN REVENUE

[ 07-08-12 0724GMT ]

Taiwan's China Steel Corp. plans to cut its utilization rate in September due to dwindling domestic demand and weaker global steel prices, a company official said Tuesday. (published 0654 GMT)

ASX Ltd., Australia's dominant exchange, is looking to rejig its grain futures contracts in a bid to capture business from the country's growing role as Asia's breadbasket, a senior executive at the exchange said Tuesday. (published 0356 GMT)

title: No Need For RBA To  Intervene  Against Strong A$ -Economists
text:
SYDNEY--Australia's central bank is unlikely to be in a mood to become the Swiss National Bank of the South Pacific and start intervening to prevent further gains in its robust currency, according to economists.

Debate about possible intervention emerged in recent weeks after former Reserve Bank of Australia board member Warwick McKibbin called publicly for the central bank to do more to limit the damage caused by the strong Australian dollar.

The strength of the Australian dollar, which is up 75% from its post-Lehman Brothers lows in 2008, has been blamed for recession-like conditions in local industries such as manufacturing.

At 0150 GMT, the Australian dollar was trading at US$1.0569, up around 10% since late May and within striking distance of its 30-year high of US$1.1080 reached a year ago.

Fanning the alarm, the Australian dollar has continued to rise in recent months despite steep falls in the prices of key commodities like iron ore and coal, a slowdown in China, and cuts in interest rates.

Since peaking in August last year, the central bank's U.S. dollar-denominated index of Australian export commodity prices has fallen 15.2%. In the same period, the CRB industrial commodity price index has fallen 23% and the price of iron ore, Australia's most important commodity export, has fallen 30%.

Currency traders say the stellar performance of the Australian dollar, the fifth most traded currency in the world, is due in part to rising demand for the country's triple-A rated sovereign bonds.

The buying by central bank reserve managers has given the Australian dollar the qualities of a reserve currency in recent years, making it less skittish in the face of commodity price volatility.

RBA Governor Glenn Stevens said in a recent speech the Australian dollar would still be prone to heavy selling in the event of a major global crisis, indicating the central bank still believes it's general behavior and tendencies haven't changed fundamentally.

"We doubt that the RBA is currently minded to become the South Pacific counterpart of the Swiss National Bank, and be prepared to intervene without limit to prevent the Australian dollar from appreciating above some chosen level," said Saul Eslake, chief economist at Merrill Lynch in Australia.

Australia, unlike Switzerland, is still experiencing the largest commodities boom in its history, and even though commodity prices appear to have peaked, the mining sector is still likely to expand further," he added.

Intervention would bring with it risks for the economy. Australia experienced mining booms before it floated its currency in 1983, all of which resulted in massive inflation spikes, Mr. Eslake added.

Cutting interest rates to lower the Australian dollar would also be bad policy, he argued.

"If cutting rates by 125 basis points (since November) has not stopped the Australian dollar from appreciating, it seems improbable that another 25 basis or 50 basis points would have any different outcome," he said.

National Australia Bank also published a comment Tuesday saying the preconditions for intervention by the RBA don't exist at the moment.

The RBA last intervened to support the Aussie dollar when the 2008 collapse of Lehman Brothers in the U.S. fueled a 40% fall in the space of weeks. The RBA will normally only intervene during periods of significant market disorder, NAB said.

"Present conditions show a relatively low and declining level of FX market volatility. There is little evidence of a disorderly market," it said.

Pushing the currency down now would only result in offering foreign buyers cheaper levels to re-enter the market, the bank said.

"In order to intervene in the FX market, the RBA may need to see a rise in market volatility," NAB said.

Write to James Glynn at james.glynn@wsj.com [ 07-08-12 0149GMT ]

title: PRESS DIGEST-Australian General News - Aug 7
text:
Compiled for Reuters by Media Monitors. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.

THE AUSTRALIAN FINANCIAL REVIEW (www.afr.com)

Former prime minister Paul Keating said at the launch of The China Choice book yesterday that the United States (US) should concentrate on strategic co-operation with China. "I have long held the view that the future of Asian stability cannot be cast by a non-Asian power - especially by the application of US military force," Mr Keating said. The view contrasts with the Federal Government's close association with the United States. Page 1.

--

Prime Minister Julia Gillard today will use a speech to an energy conference to intensify pressure on the state governments to revamp electricity markets. Observers said the address was a tactic to shift blame on recent energy price rises from the Federal Government's carbon tax to the "gold-plating" of transmission networks. "Prices have gone up far and fast. The last four years' price rises cannot continue  for too long, some state governments have been increasing their revenue at the expense of the family electricity bill - that has to stop," Ms Gillard will say. Page 1.

--

Federal Opposition treasury spokesman Joe Hockey yesterday said the Coalition, if elected, would extend a banking inquiry to cover the A$1.8 trillion funds management industry because of its importance to Australia. "There is a structural risk associated with superannuation because of its sheer scale over the next 10 to 15 years  there is going to be more money in superannuation and funds under management than there is in the banking system," Mr Hockey said. Page 1.

--

Joe Hockey, treasury spokesman for the Federal Opposition, yesterday indicated that the Coalition would not support the Reserve Bank of Australiaintervening in the Australian dollar. Warwick McKibbin, a former member of the central bank's board, yesterday wrote in a newspaper column that the Reserve Bank should print money to stymie foreign demand for the currency. "I respect Professor McKibbin, but I don't necessarily agree with everything he says," Mr Hockey stated. Page 3.

--

THE AUSTRALIAN (www.theaustralian.news.com.au)

The latest opinion poll by researchers Newspoll has recorded a 5 percent surge in support for the Federal Government, giving it its highest rating since February. Labor's 33 percent rating, however, still trails the Coalition's 45 percent, with the latter also maintaining a 54 percent to 46 percent lead on the two-party preferred vote. Respondents also preferred Federal Opposition Leader Tony Abbott to Prime Minister Julia Gillard as leader by 38 percent to 36 percent. Page 1.

--

A review of the Australian Labor Party's catastrophic campaign at this year's Queensland state election has found that the party had "left behind traditional supporters and allies". Conducted by former New South Wales deputy premier Carmel Tebbutt, former Keating government minister Michael Lee and party national secretary George Wright, the inquiry recommended that the party boost its relationship with unions, revamp its policy platform and reconnect with the ethnic vote. Page 1.

--

New South Wales and Victoria yesterday strongly criticised the Murray-Darling Basin Authority's revised plan for the river system, accusing the Federal Government of opening up regional areas to economic hardship and ignoring potential water savings. Federal Water Minister Tony Burke yesterday admitted that the authority's plan "falls short of the environmental objectives I hope to achieve" but the current version was an improvement. The plan aims to return thousands of gigalitres to the basin to restore its health. Page 1.

--

Brian Wilson, chairman of the Foreign Investment Review Board, yesterday said that sovereign wealth funds and state-owned corporations must not have political motivations when acquiring Australian assets or companies. "Australian businesses, however they are owned, should be run on a purely commercial basis and not as an extension of the policy, political or economic agenda of a foreign government," Mr Wilson said. Page 1.

--

THE SYDNEY MORNING HERALD (www.smh.com.au)

The former New South Wales Australian Labor Party ministers will front an Independent Commission Against Corruption hearing tomorrow to answer questions surrounding the granting of coal exploration licences by former mining minister Ian Macdonald's department later this year. Along with Mr Macdonald, state MP Eric Roozendaal and controversial factional leader Eddie Obeid will also appear before the public inquiry, which will examine instances such as the granting of several licences to a company worth A$1. Page 1.

--

The Federal Opposition is formulating a plan to compensate farmers to store carbon in their fields for 25 years as part of its climate change policy. Current greenhouse schemes dictate that any land set aside for reducing carbon be left as such for 100 years, but the Coalition's Greg Hunt said the shorter abatement period offered farmers a choice that "didn't lock up land for generations". Martijn Wilder, partner at law firm Baker and McKenzie, said the Coalition was "either banking on the idea that in 25 years the problem will have gone away" or an alternative solution will be found. Page 2.

--

One of the new cameras designed to catch criminals in Sydney's Kings Cross has already assisted in the arrest of an offender a day after its installation. A spokesperson for the City of Sydney Council yesterday said that "an attempted bag snatch" was captured by the closed-circuit television camera on Friday afternoon. "Staff in the city's security control room fed the images in real time to Kings Cross police, who detained a suspect a short time later," the spokesperson added. Page 2.

--

Richard Woodward, vice-president of the Australian and International Pilots Association, yesterday said that he did not believe the Civil Aviation Safety Authority's random screening for drugs and alcohol required an overhaul because the level of positive tests in the local aviation sector were "infinitesimally low". "The pilots, as a body, are healthier than they have ever been. Sure, they might meet in a bar for a drink before they go to dinner  but I would put that in perspective," Mr Woodward said. Page 2.

--

THE AGE (www.theage.com.au("http://www.theage.com.au"))

Sally Pearson yesterday said that she didn't realise her 12.58 second run in the heats of the 100 metre hurdles was the fastest heat time in the Olympics until she reached the mixed zone. "I had no idea. It is good but I am sort of oblivious to those things and just going in there fresh and calm and ready to go," the Australian hurdler and world champion said. "I am just going to get my recovery done and make sure I get something to eat, have some nice cold baths and watch some," she added. Page 1.

--

Champion jockey Mark Zahra has become involved in the Smoking Aces race-fixing scandal over allegations that he conspired to ride his horse, Baikal, in a manner that limited the chances of the race favourite, Retaliate. Mr Zahra, one of Australia's leading jockeys, and fellow rider Danny Nikolic have both refused to answer questions into the incident, which was uncovered during a police investigation into the murder of former horse trainer Les Samba last year. Page 1.

--

A price index compiled by financial services group TD Securities and researchers Melbourne Institute has found that the impact of the Federal Government's carbon tax has been minimal, with the cost of living benchmark increasing by an overall 0.2 percent in July. Economist Stephen Koukoulas, who was responsib [20120806 203403 GMT]

le for creating the index, said that inflation would have fallen by 0.2 percent last month without the introduction of the carbon tax. Annette Beacher, research chief at TD Securities, forecast that future effects of the impost would be reduced. Page 2.

--

A study by the University of New England and the Australian Institute of Family Studies has found that a third of Australian kids aged older than 2 are spending more than two hours a day watching television. The joint review also discovered that children from poorer socio-economic backgrounds tended to watch more television. Dr Ben Edwards, researcher at the institute, said the findings could explain why "social advantage is transmitted across generations" because excessive viewing of television could hamper a child's development and learning. Page 3.
