title: UPDATE: Australia  Central Bank  Chief Endorses Strong  Currency
text:
--RBA chief warns against wishing for a weaker exchange rate

--Says Aussie dollar strength a boon for consumers

--Urges struggling businesses to adapt to exchange rate

(Recasts lead, adds comment from RBA Governor Glenn Stevens from third paragraph.)

By Enda Curran

SYDNEY--The strong Australian dollar is helping spread the benefits of a once-in-a-century mining boom by boosting the purchasing power of consumers, the head of the country's central bank said Wednesday.

In his strongest endorsement yet of the strength of the exchange rate, Reserve Bank of Australia Governor Glenn Stevens used an economic forum hosted by Prime Minister Julia Gillard to urge exporters and manufacturers to skill up and adapt their business models to cope with the impact of the high currency.

"While I'm very conscious a number of sectors are struggling with the exchange rate where it is, we shouldn't wish too quickly for a low exchange rate," Mr Stevens said.

"Every time we put petrol in our car, every time we go to a store and buy consumer durables or clothing, a lot of which is imported, every time we travel overseas we are benefiting from the high exchange rate, and indeed as consumers the exchange rate is one of the devices that is imparting to us the higher wealth that the mining boom brings," said Mr Stevens.

That blunt message runs directly into complaints from trade unions, corporate leaders and others that the Australian dollar is killing off the non-mining sectors of the economy and forcing some companies to relocate production offshore.

Record high prices for commodities exports such as coal and iron ore continue to fuel the Australian economy, which was the fastest growing in the developed world in the first three months of 2012, and has close to full employment levels.

Those high export prices--which have cooled from their peaks but remain strong--have pushed the Australian dollar to record highs against rival currencies, hurting exporters and manufacturers and sparking worries that the economy outside of the mining sector is being hollowed out.

Since the depths of the 2008 global financial crisis, the Aussie dollar has rebounded by 70% against the greenback and continues to trade around parity, even as the world economy and commodities prices show signs of cooling.

To offset those pains, the central bank has eased policy by 125 basis points since November, but so far the currency is continuing to hold up.

Speaking at a government forum designed to address the impact of the currency, Mr. Stevens urged business leaders to focus on productivity and help lift Australia in the global rankings. It currently lies in 15th place in the IMD World Competitiveness Indicator, behind other resource-rich nations such as Qatar, Norway and Canada.

"The test is how many of those enterprise can get the productivity up because that's really the way out in terms of coping with a high exchange rate," Mr. Stevens said. "Are we really going to compete with Asia with our wages? Well, we're not, and there's no point pretending we can."

"What we have to do is compete with higher productivity," he said.

Australia's central bank rarely intervenes to adjust the strength of the exchange rate, and says publicly it only does so to smooth liquidity during times of volatile price movements. The currency was freely floated in 1983.

Write to Enda Curran at enda.curran@wsj.com [ 13-06-12 0104GMT ]

title: 3rd UPDATE: Asian Shares Edge Lower After China Trade Data
text:
-- Nikkei down 0.4%, Hang Seng Index down 0.5%, S&P ASX 200 up 0.5%

-- Rupee climbs after government intervention

(Recasts 1st paragraph, updates prices, adds paragraphs on Australia, rupee, adds quotes)

By Daniel Inman

Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES

HONG KONG (Dow Jones)--Asian markets edged lower after disappointing China trade data, while India's rupee rallied after the government imposed foreign-exchange restrictions aimed at halting the currency's recent slump.

The Nikkei fell 0.4% to 9009.65 after earlier dropping below the 9000 level, the first time since February. Korea's KOSPI fell 0.3% to 1944.93. Australia's S&P ASX 200 rose 0.5% to 4295.60 as the Australian dollar touched its lowest level for five months as risk aversion spurred investors to move away from higher-yielding currencies.

Hong Kong's Hang Seng Index was down 0.5% at 20227.28 and the China Shanghai SE Composite closed flat at 2410.23.

Although ongoing coalition talks in Greece and the high cost of Spanish borrowing remained a concern, markets initially struggled to find a direction in early trade. Markets started to fall after China posted a wider trade surplus due to weak imports, reflecting sluggish performance in the world's second biggest economy. A 4.9% increase in exports and 0.3% increase in imports both failed to meet economist expectations. China will release more data on Friday, including industrial output, retail sales, and inflation data.

After hitting its lowest level since January overnight, the euro was able to regain some ground against the dollar, up 0.1% at $1.2950. The yen stayed flat against the dollar, trading at the 79.715 level. The price of oil fell 0.4%, to $96.47 barrel.

The Australian dollar fell to a five-month low of 1.0029 before climbing back to 1.0119. Combined with upbeat employment data, the S&P ASX 200 was able to claw back 0.5% at the close, after hitting a four-week low on Wednesday. Mining stocks staged a recovery. Newcrest Mining was up 5.6% and Iluka Resources climbed 5.8%.

"All the shipwrecks of the past few days are finding support as the Australian dollar falls," said Macquarie Private Wealth investment advisor John Milroy.

In India, the central bank stepped in to halt a slide in the rupee by imposing foreign-exchange restrictions on companies and tightening the trading rules for banks. The measures provided a boost to the currency, pushing the dollar down to an intraday low of 52.94. It recently traded at 53.29.

The Nikkei started Thursday by touching an intraday low of 8985.90. It has dropped 12% from its year-to-date high in March.

The decline in the market coincides with a strengthening of the yen against the dollar, making Japanese exports less competitive. Some analysts also say the Nikkei's rally early this year, rising 19% in the first quarter, was overdone.

Continuing the trend of Japanese companies offering healthy forecasts, Toyota Motor Corp rose 0.8% after it released operating profit guidance of Y1 trillion for the year ending March. The numbers met market expectations, and analysts note that the carmaker tends to make conservative targets.

Cathay Pacific Airways Ltd. fell 6.3% after warning late Wednesday that first-half financial results will be "disappointing" as high fuel costs persist, prompting the airline to cut flights and seek cost cuts.

title: DJ  Australia 's Lowe Says A$  Intervention  Unlikely
text:
SYDNEY (Dow Jones)--Australia's dollar is fairly valued and the country's economic health means that it's difficult for the Reserve Bank of Australia to justify intervention under current conditions, said the deputy governor Wednesday.

In a statement that will add to the concerns of manufacturers and home owners, Philip Lowe said strong employment data, projections for growth around trend and an inflation rate within the bank's 2-3% target means the strong Aussie dollar doesn't merit an attempt to weaken it.

"While ever that is the case I think it is difficult to make a strong argument that the exchange rate is fundamentally misaligned and while ever that is the case that makes the hurdle for intervention quite high," Lowe said in a question and answer session after a speech.

The central bank only intervenes when the currency is clearly over valued, Lowe said.

"Our general strategy here is to only do so when the currency is clearly away from levels that could be justified by fundamentals," Lowe said.

"At the moment, the high currency is being driven by the high terms of trade and the higher terms of trade are being driven by these global developments so I don't think we can make the case that the currency is fundamentally away from where the right level is."

"That's always an issue that we keep under consideration. It's possible that it would move outside the range that is justified by the terms of trade but I think on the basis of all the work we have done so far it would be difficult to make the case the exchange rate is fundamentally too high at the moment."

title: Australia  Central Bank  Says Policy Right For Now
text:
--RBA Governor Happy With Current Interest Rate Settings

--RBA Governor Says Rates Remain Under Review

--RBA Governor Doesn't Rule Out Australian Dollar Intervention

SYDNEY -- Interest rates in Australia look set to remain unchanged for now after the central bank said Friday current policy setting are "about right", albeit they are constantly reviewed especially in light of Europe's troubles which are likely to be long lasting.

"Our most recent assessment was that, with growth near trend, inflation consistent with the target, interest rates about average, and an outlook suggesting more of the same, the setting of policy was about right for the moment," Reserve Bank of Australia Governor Glenn Stevens told parliament.

"Of course, we continue to reassess things each month," he added.

With the Australian dollar soaring and creating problems for exporters, Stevens said the RBA was mindful of the changes underway in the economy adding he would never rule out intervention to lower the currency.

"I am not attracted to attempting to do that at the moment because I am not sure it would be effective," he said.

The Australian dollar is close to 80% above the lows it hit in late 2008 after the collapse of Lehman Brothers. The rise, fueled by a once-in-a-century mining boom, has crippled manufactured exports and slugged key industries like tourism.

"We haven't done any intervention to try to hold the Australian dollar down. I'm not saying we never would, we have been known to intervene on both sides but we certainly don't foreshadow it," he said.

"I'm not saying we would never do it but we haven't done so to date, but we do continue to ask ourselves whether what's happening in the currency makes sense," Stevens added.

The Australian dollar was up slightly after Stevens' comments. At 0030 GMT, it was trading at A$1.0729.

Overall, Stevens said he remained upbeat on the outlook for the economy, saying the country's banks are in good shape and there is policy ammunition available if the world growth outlook turns down.

-By James Glynn, Dow Jones Newswires; 61-2-8272-4685; james.glynn@dowjones.com [ 02-23-12 1915ET ]

title: DJ RBA Governor Not Attracted To A$  Intervention  Right Now
text:
SYDNEY (Dow Jones)--Australia's central bank governor said Friday he isn't attracted to the idea of intervening to weaken the Australian dollar but the bank does retain it as an option.

The Australian dollar has surged in recent years and remains well above parity against the greenback, hurting trade-exposed sectors such as tourism and manufacturing. It is trading around US$1.0728.

Reserve Bank of Australia Governor Glenn Stevens said the example of Switzerland which placed a cap on the Swiss Franc doesn't apply to Australia as the countries are experiencing different economic conditions.

"The exchange rate forces acting there are more powerful I would say than what we faced," Stevens told a parliamentary hearing.

"I am not attracted to attempting to do that at the moment because I am not sure it would be effective. We haven't done any intervention to try to hold the Australian dollar down. I'm not saying we never would, we have been known to intervene on both sides but we certainly don't foreshadow it," he said.

"I'm not saying we would never do it but we haven't done so to date, but we do continue to ask ourselves whether what's happening in the currency makes sense," Stevens said.

"I would observe the most recent bout of strength is happening at a time when the terms of trade has peaked and is starting to come down, that is a bit odd but we will see what happens," he added.

title: DJ  Australia 's  Central Bank  Highlights Limits Of  FX Intervention
text:
SYDNEY (Dow Jones)--Central bank intervention in foreign exchange markets has only short-lived results that are of limited value, according to a report from the Reserve Bank of Australia released Thursday.

The report reviews each period of intervention by the Reserve Bank of Australia since the nation's currency was floated in 1983. It says the foreign-exchange market has evolved to where participants are now better equipped to manage their own risk. As a result, intervention has become less frequent and more targeted, and should be reserved chiefly for periods of market dysfunction.

The bank, using regression analysis, also gauges the effectiveness of its past interventions, concluding that the results illustrate the inherent limitations of intervention, which it says policymakers need to be aware of.

"When foreign exchange markets are deep and liquid (and the capital account is open), the effects of intervention on the level of the exchange rate are generally short-lived," it said.

"Moreover, under these 'normal' circumstances, the practical difficulties involved in determining what the 'fair value' of an exchange rate should be, suggest that it is difficult for policymakers to systematically improve on market outcomes, particularly in real time."

But the central bank says intervention can play an important role in periods of severe market dysfunction, where it may become an important stabilizing force.

The bank said it last intervened in the currency markets between October and November 2008, in the aftermath of the collapse of U.S. investment bank Lehman Brother's. It intervened nine times in that period, with prices between US$0.6000 and US$0.7700. The average size of the daily interventions at that time was 0.47% of daily turnover.

Some policymakers called on the Reserve Bank of Australia to intervene in currency markets as the Australian dollar surged to 30-year highs earlier this year, above US$1.1000. The central bank argued that its policy was to intervene only when the market wasn't functioning appropriately.
